info.title: API
info.description:
The product's HTTP API. The request and response shapes described here are the
same ones used by every other way into the product — the MCP tools, the webhook
bodies, the WebSocket payloads — so learning this document is enough for all of
them.

**Start here:** [Quickstart](#quickstart) · [Authentication](#authentication) ·
[Connecting an agent](#connecting-an-agent) ·
[Tenants and organizations](#tenants-and-organizations) ·
[Pages and filters](#pages-and-filters) ·
[Dates and times](#dates-and-times) ·
[Retrying a write safely](#retrying-a-write-safely) ·
[Errors](#errors) · [Consuming webhooks](#consuming-webhooks) ·
[Events and other ways in](#events-and-other-ways-in) ·
[Changelog and deprecation policy](#changelog-and-deprecation-policy).
Everything after that is the reference: one entry per operation, with what to
send, what comes back, and every way it can be refused.

## Quickstart

Get a token, make a call, follow an id.

**1. Get a token.** Sign in at `/accounts/login/` — if you do not know where
your organization signs in, `POST /api/v1/auth/realm/` takes an email address
and answers before you have any credential. Then, still signed in, mint one —
`POST /tokens/` — from your browser's devtools console:

    await fetch("/api/v1/tokens/", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "X-CSRFToken": document.cookie.match(/csrftoken=([^;]+)/)[1],
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({name: "quickstart", scopes: ["widgets:read"]}),
    }).then(r => r.json())

Minting takes a signed-in browser session plus that `X-CSRFToken` header — a
bearer token cannot mint another token. `scopes` has no default; omitting it is
refused. Ask for the narrowest set the job needs: every operation below names
the scope it wants, a section's write scope includes the read, and `["*"]`
means no limit at all.

**The token is in this one response and is never shown again** — save it now.
Read `effective_scopes` in the same response: it is the part of what you asked
for that your role can actually back, so a scope that would have been dead
weight shows up here rather than as a refusal later.

**2. Make a call.** Send the token on every request:

    curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/widgets/ \
         -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Every list answers the same envelope:

    {"items": [ ... ], "has_more": false, "next_cursor": null, "count": null}

**3. Follow an id.** Take an `id` out of `items` and ask for that row:

    curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/widgets/$ID/ \
         -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

That is the shape of the whole API: a list you walk by following
`next_cursor`, and an `id` you follow to the single-item route.

**Next:** [Pages and filters](#pages-and-filters) for the rest of the list
controls · [Errors](#errors) for the refusal envelope ·
[Connecting an agent](#connecting-an-agent) to drive all of this through
`/mcp`.

## Authentication

Two credentials are accepted everywhere: a **bearer token**
(`Authorization: Bearer <token>`) for a program, and a **browser session
cookie** for a signed-in page. Send one, not both.

**A `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` made with a session cookie must also
carry the value of the `csrftoken` cookie in an `X-CSRFToken` header** — a
cookie is sent by the browser whether or not the page meant it. A bearer token
needs nothing extra.

Mint a token with `POST /tokens/`. It belongs to one person, is pinned to one
tenant, and minting needs a browser session — a token cannot mint another
token, because the offspring would outlive its parent's revocation. Revoke one
with `DELETE /tokens/{id}/`: immediate, and the record stays, so the audit
trail still says what that token did.

**Every token carries a scope list**, asked for at the mint. A scope is a
section of this API followed by `:read` or `:write`, and each operation below
says which one it needs. Within a section the write scope includes the read —
one way only, and never across sections. A scope only narrows: the minter's
role still decides underneath, so ask for the narrowest set that does the job.
A call outside the token's list is refused with `insufficient_scope` naming
the missing scope. `["*"]` says out loud that a token should have no limit at
all.

A request with no usable credential answers `401` before anything else is
considered. That is not one of the refusals an operation lists, because
nothing about the caller has been decided yet.

### The two planes

The sections of this API fall into two planes, and **which plane you can
change things in is decided by your role in the tenant, not by your token** —
a scope narrows what your role already allows, never widens it. Ask for a
scope your role cannot back and the mint does not refuse you: it hands back a
narrower `effective_scopes`, which is why that field is worth reading — an
ordinary member asking for an administrative section's write scope is handed
that section's read scope instead.

**The everyday plane** is the product itself, plus the parts of the platform
that are about you. An ordinary member of a tenant reads and writes here all
day and never meets a `403`.

* `devices` — the push address book: the handsets and browsers a contact has let this product notify. Its own section rather than a corner of `messaging`, because the two are not the same trust — a client trusted to register the phone it is running on is not thereby trusted to mail everybody in the contact book, and a mobile app's token can hold this section's write half and nothing else. Registering says the product **can** reach a handset and never that it **may**: consent, quiet hours and suppression for the `push` channel live with the other consent verbs under `messaging`, and every notification is checked against them. Write-only in practice — a registration door and a retirement door, both addressed by the id the first hands back — so this section's read half reaches nothing, exactly as Usage's write half does.
* `djb_imports` — bringing rows in from a CSV file: stage it, read the preview, apply it. Everyday rather than administrative, because an import makes exactly the rows you could make one at a time — and it asks, for every row, the same permission making that row by hand would.
* `djb_notes` — write a note about a record, read a record's notes, correct your own, archive one that no longer belongs.
* `djb_tags` — the tenant's shared words and the rows that carry them: tag a row you can see, read a row's tags, take a tag off. Everyday, because tagging is ordinary work and every link lives in the branch its row lives in. **Coining, renaming, archiving and restoring a word take an administrator of the whole tenant**, because a word means the same thing in every branch, and they are refused with `403 forbidden` otherwise.
* `exports` — taking a copy of your data out: ask for an archive of everything your organization can see, follow it while it is built, and download it. Everyday rather than administrative, because an export of your own organization contains exactly what you can already read one page at a time. Asking for the **whole account** is the one act here that takes an owner or an administrator of it, and it is refused with `403 forbidden` otherwise.
* `files` — documents you store with us and the versions they have had: put one in, replace it later without losing what it used to say, and fetch any version back on a short-lived private link. **The bytes never travel through this API** — you upload and download straight to storage on links we sign and record. Everyday rather than administrative, because filing and replacing are ordinary product work and what you can see is already narrowed to the part of the tree you are acting in. **Archiving is the one act here that takes an owner or an administrator**, because it takes a document out of everybody's working set while the stored bytes remain, and it is refused with `403 forbidden` otherwise.
* `messaging` — sending a message to somebody, and the contact book that records who may be contacted and how.
* `portal_requests` — send a request about a widget, list the requests you can see, read one.
* `runs` — the background jobs: work the API started rather than finished while you waited. Anybody in the tenant can read the ledger; you can replay a run you started yourself.
* `search` — finding things by typing words. One endpoint covers every kind of record this product has made searchable, and answers with pointers you fetch in full through that record's own section. Everyday rather than administrative, and read-only: what a search can find is exactly what you could already page through, and nothing writes to the index through a door.
* `socket-tickets` — the one-use ticket that opens this tenant's event socket.
* `tokens` — your own API tokens: mint one, revoke one. Nothing reads a token's secret back; you can only ever revoke your own.
* `usage` — what your organization has consumed, meter by meter, with the daily subtotals each total was added up from. Everyday rather than administrative for the same reason `exports` is: a report covers the part of the tree you are acting in, so it tells you nothing you could not have added up yourself from the rows you can already read. **Read-only, and it is the one section with no write side at all** — consumption is recorded by the platform as it happens, so a write half reaches nothing and nobody needs to ask for it.
* `widgets` — the worked example resource, and the shape every product resource follows: list it, filter it, create one, follow an id.

**The administrative plane** is the tenant's own configuration. **Reading here
is open to anybody in the tenant**, narrowed as usual to the part of the tree
you are acting in. **Changing any of it takes an owner or an administrator**;
a member who tries is refused with `403 forbidden` saying which act was
refused.

* `auth` — how this tenant signs people in, and which identity providers it trusts. `POST /auth/realm/` answers before anybody is signed in: it says where an email address should go.
* `connections` — this tenant's links to outside systems, the credentials behind them, and the signed webhooks those systems send in.
* `events` — webhook subscriptions: where this tenant's events are delivered, and what became of each delivery.
* `invitations` — bringing somebody in: issuing an invitation at a branch and a role, revoking one, and the link that accepts it.
* `org-structure` — the tenant's organization tree: its branches, how they nest, and what each one is called. The structure only; who is in it is `roles`.
* `roles` — who belongs to which part of the tenant, and as what. Kept apart from the tree it is granted against, so a credential trusted to reshape the structure is not thereby trusted to promote anybody.
* `tenant-settings` — the tenant's name, time zone, locale, feature switches and the free-form settings object.
* `users` — taking a person's access away: deactivation, which is reversible, and erasure, which is not. You may always act on your own account.

Two edges. A section in the everyday plane can still hold an administrator's
operation, and each such operation says so in its own description. And the
plane decides which refusal you meet: an act refused *on something you can
see* is `403 forbidden`; anything you were not allowed to see in the first
place is `404 not_found`, as
[Tenants and organizations](#tenants-and-organizations) explains.

## Connecting an agent

**This product ships a machine door and a map to drive it with, and no agent
of its own.** Bring the assistant you already use.

**The door is `/mcp`** — one Streamable-HTTP endpoint speaking the Model
Context Protocol. It takes the same bearer token as everything else, and the
same `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` headers:

    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "example": {
          "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp",
          "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer $TOKEN"}
        }
      }
    }

**The map is `/llms.txt`** — this same contract as flat text, generated when
you ask for it, so it cannot go stale. Hand it to an agent that is deciding
*which* call to make: every operation with its prose, the credential it wants,
the scope it needs and the ways it can refuse, plus the whole scope vocabulary
in one block. Far smaller than the OpenAPI document, and no JavaScript.

**A worked example.** Mint a token scoped to the one job — say `widgets:read`
and nothing else — point the agent at `/mcp` with it, and ask a question in
words. The agent finds `list_widgets`, calls it, and walks the pages by
handing back the `next_cursor` it was given. Same operation, same shapes and
same refusals as `GET /api/v1/widgets/`; every capability in this document is
a tool at `/mcp` unless its own description says why not.

**The tool list does not shrink to fit the token's scopes.** An out-of-scope
tool is still listed, and refuses when called, with `insufficient_scope`
naming the missing scope. Hiding it would teach the agent that the capability
does not exist — false, and unfixable, because nobody would learn which scope
to ask for. Refusing names the one that can.

## Tenants and organizations

Data here belongs to a **tenant** — one customer account — and each tenant is
a **tree of organizations**, so a large customer can keep its divisions,
regions or franchisees apart inside one account. Two optional headers say
where in that structure you are acting. Both are re-checked against your
memberships on every request, so neither can reach anything you were not
already allowed to see.

* **`X-Tenant: <slug>`** — which customer account. Leave it out and you act in
  the one your account defaults to. **Name one your credential cannot act in
  and the request is refused** — `403 addressing_header_not_honoured`, naming
  the header — rather than quietly answering with nothing in it. A header you
  sent is a header you meant, so a template that did not interpolate is told
  so instead of reading as an empty account.
* **`X-Org: <slug>`** — which organization inside that tenant: one you are a
  member of, or one below your membership. Leave it out and you act in the
  organization your membership names. Permissions run **downwards only**:
  acting as an organization shows you its own data and that of everything
  beneath it, never a neighbouring organization's and never its parent's.

**Anything you are not allowed to see answers `404 not_found`, not
`403 forbidden`** — so a `404` is never proof that something does not exist.
Do not build a client that treats it as one.

## Pages and filters

Every list route answers the same envelope and takes the same controls, so a
client that has learned one list has learned all of them:

    {"items": [ ... ], "has_more": true, "next_cursor": "eyJ2IjoxLCJ0Ijoi...", "count": null}

**Walk a list by following `next_cursor`.** Ask for the first page with no
cursor; while `has_more` is true, send the `next_cursor` you were just given
back as `?cursor=`. When `has_more` is false, `next_cursor` is `null` and you
have seen everything.

    GET /api/v1/widgets/
    GET /api/v1/widgets/?cursor=eyJ2IjoxLCJ0Ijoi...

* **`?cursor=`** — where to carry on from. **It is opaque**: signed, tied to
  the account and the sort order it was issued for, and not a page number in
  disguise. Never build one, edit one, or keep one across a change of
  `?ordering=` — an edited or replayed cursor is refused with
  `400 invalid_cursor`.
* **`?limit=`** — how many items to return, up to the maximum the schema
  publishes (`maximum` on this parameter). **Ask for more and the request is
  refused**, `400 invalid`, naming the field — you are never quietly given the
  maximum instead, because a page of 200 returned to a request for 5000 is
  indistinguishable from a list that had 200 items in it, and a client walking
  by that answer stops at the first page.
* **`?include_count=true`** — adds `count`, the exact number of matching items
  across the whole list. **Without it, `count` is `null`**: counting costs a
  second pass over the matches, so you pay for a total only where you display
  one.
* **`?ordering=`** — a field name, with `-` in front of it for descending.
  Each list states which fields it accepts; anything else is refused rather
  than ignored.
* **`?q=`** — free-text search, where the list says it is supported.

**There is no page number.** A list here is newest-first, so with offsets one
item created or removed while you read shifts everything after it, and page 2
silently skips or repeats an item — an answer that looks exactly like a
correct page. A cursor names a position, not a count. It does not promise a
frozen snapshot: an item added above where you are is not on this walk — start
again to see it — and an item edited into a position you have passed will not
come round again. What it removes is skipping an item you never saw.

Lists take filters of their own as well, named in each operation. A filter the
route does not accept is refused with `400 invalid`, so a typo in a filter
name never silently returns the unfiltered list.

## Dates and times

Every instant this API returns is **UTC, ISO-8601, to the millisecond**:

    "created_at": "2026-08-25T09:30:00.123Z"

**The same row read through the machine door at `/mcp` carries the same
string, byte for byte.** One encoder renders both doors, so a client may
compare two renderings of a row for equality, key a cache on one, or diff a
REST answer against a tool result without normalising anything first. Three
fractional digits is the contract, not an accident of whichever library
serialised the answer.

Send times the same way. A field named `_at` is an instant and a field named
`_on` is a calendar date (`"2026-08-25"`), which is the difference between
"when it happened" and "which day it belongs to".

## Retrying a write safely

Send **`Idempotency-Key: <a key you choose>`** on any `POST`, `PUT` or
`PATCH`. The first request under a key runs and its response is remembered.
Repeat the request **byte-identically** under the same key and you get that
same response back, marked with **`Idempotent-Replayed: true`** — the write does
not happen twice. Use a new random key per logical operation; reuse it only when
retrying that operation.

**Byte-identical means what it says.** The match is over the method, the path
and the raw body, so re-serialising the same data — a pretty-printer, a
different key order, an SDK that rebuilds the body on retry — is a DIFFERENT
request under a key that is already spoken for, and it is refused rather than
replayed. Retry by sending the bytes you sent the first time; keep the encoded
body if your client rebuilds it.

Two things are refused rather than guessed at:

* the same key with a **different body** — `409 idempotency_key_reuse`.
  Nothing was written. Pick a new key if you meant a new operation.
* a retry arriving while the **first one is still running** — `409
  in_progress`. Wait a moment and retry; the answer is not lost.

## Errors

Every refusal has the same JSON shape, whatever went wrong:

    {
      "detail": "No widget matches that id.",
      "code": "not_found",
      "remedies": [{"label": "List what you can see", "destination": "docs:openapi"}]
    }

* `detail` — a sentence saying what happened;
* `code` — a short stable string such as `not_found`. Branch on this, never on
  the status code or the wording;
* `errors` — present when the problem is with particular fields: an object of
  field name to a list of messages;
* `remedies` — what you can do about it, each with a label and where to go.

Each operation lists the codes it can answer with, so a client can be written
against that exact set rather than against every code in the API.

## Consuming webhooks

**This section is about the webhooks we send you.** Register a URL, and every
time an event you subscribed to happens, we POST the payload to it — the same
shape the matching REST route returns.

**1. Subscribe.** `POST /webhook-endpoints/` with your URL and the event names
you want; `GET /event-types/` lists every name this deployment can send,
derived from what the product actually declares. **The response to the
registration is the only place your signing secret is ever shown** — save it
then. If you lose it, `POST /webhook-endpoints/{id}/secret/` issues a new one
and the old one stops verifying at the next delivery.

**2. Verify every delivery.** Each one arrives with two signature headers,
both keyed on your secret. Check either. **Prefer `X-Signature-V2`.**

`X-Signature-V2: t=<unix seconds>,sha256=<hex>` — join the number after `t=`
to the **exact bytes of the body** with a single `.` between them, HMAC-SHA256
that with your secret, and compare it with the value after `sha256=` in
constant time. Then check that `t` is within **5 minutes** of your own clock.
Both checks must pass:

    import hashlib, hmac, time

    def verify_v2(secret: str, body: bytes, header: str) -> bool:
        parts = dict(p.split("=", 1) for p in header.split(","))
        signed_at, sent = int(parts["t"]), parts["sha256"]
        if abs(time.time() - signed_at) > 300:
            return False
        payload = str(signed_at).encode() + b"." + body
        mine = hmac.new(secret.encode(), payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        return hmac.compare_digest(mine, sent)

`X-Signature: sha256=<hex>` — the original scheme: HMAC-SHA256 of the exact
body bytes, hex-encoded, prefixed with `sha256=`. It signs no timestamp, so a
copy of one delivery verifies against it for as long as your secret lives —
the time check is the reason to move. It is still sent on every delivery and
will not be withdrawn without notice:

    def verify_v1(secret: str, body: bytes, header: str) -> bool:
        mine = hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        return hmac.compare_digest("sha256=" + mine, header)

For either scheme: **hash the bytes you received.** Parsing the JSON and
re-encoding it changes the bytes, and the signature will not match.

**3. Ignore what you have already seen.** Every delivery carries `X-Event-Id`,
**stable across retries and replays** — the same event sent again is the same
id. Record the ids you have processed and drop a repeat. Do not use `t` for
this: every attempt is signed at the moment it is sent, so a retry an hour
later carries a fresh `t` and a genuine signature. Deliveries also carry
`X-Event-Name` and `X-Correlation-Id`.

**4. Answer quickly, and know the retry schedule.** Any 2xx means accepted.
Anything else, or no answer at all, is a failure we retry:

* each attempt gets **15 seconds** to answer;
* we make up to **6 attempts** in all;
* the first retry follows about **2 seconds** later and each wait doubles,
  never going above **5 minutes** between attempts;
* the whole conversation about one delivery stops **1 hour** after it started.

So answer `202` from the front of your handler and do the work afterwards — a
receiver that finishes its own slow work before replying is how a healthy
integration starts failing under load.

**5. Read what happened, and replay what we gave up on.** `GET /deliveries/`
lists every delivery with its status, its attempt count, and what your server
last answered — when it answered at all. A delivery that survives the whole
schedule without being accepted is **dead-lettered**: nothing is retrying it
any more, and it appears in `GET /dead-letters/`. When you have fixed whatever
was wrong, `POST /dead-letters/{id}/replay/` sends it again — **to every
endpoint subscribed to that event, including ones that already received it**,
which is the other reason step 3 matters.

**Testing locally.** Register an endpoint pointing at a tunnel to your laptop,
make the change that fires the event, then watch `GET /deliveries/`: it says
whether we called you, what you answered and how many attempts are left.
Before there is anything to tunnel to, test the verifier alone: sign a body
with your own secret, check your verifier says yes, then change one byte and
check that it says no.

## Events and other ways in

* **Outbound webhooks** — see [Consuming webhooks](#consuming-webhooks).
  `GET /event-types/` lists every event name you can subscribe to.
* **MCP** — see [Connecting an agent](#connecting-an-agent): one
  Streamable-HTTP endpoint at **`/mcp`**, the same bearer token, the same
  headers, and every capability in this document as a tool.
* **WebSockets** — connect to `/ws/events/` to receive those same payloads as
  they happen, in the same shapes this document describes. A socket shows you
  what is happening while you are connected; a webhook is what reaches you
  when you are not.

## Changelog and deprecation policy

Every surface in this document is generated from the deployment that serves
it — this page, `openapi.json`, and `/llms.txt` — so the reference is never a
description of an older version of itself. Fetch `openapi.json` on a schedule
and diff it: a changelog that cannot disagree with what is running.

**What may appear without notice:** new operations, new sections, new
optional request fields, and new fields on a response. Write a client that
ignores fields it does not recognise and never treats an enum's value set as
exhaustive, and none of them will break it.

### Versioning

The version is in the path: **`/api/v1/`**. A breaking change arrives as a
`/v2/` alongside this one, and `/v1/` keeps answering until clients have
moved. Within a version, a field is never removed from a response, and never
changes type.

That promise runs from **2026-08-24**, the day list responses moved to cursors
and this API acquired its first outside consumer; the one change it does not
cover is that move itself. An exception to the promise is dated, in
writing, in this section — that paragraph is the only one there is. A change
that would need a second one is a `/v2/` instead.

### What a /v2/ would mean

`/v2/` is a **second path that answers alongside this one**, not a switch that
gets thrown. Removing a field, changing a field's type, or changing what an
operation means are the changes that earn one. When one arrives, `/v1/` keeps
answering while clients move, this page says so, and the date `/v1/` stops
being served is published before it happens.

A section name — which is half of every scope your tokens carry — and a URL
path are the same kind of promise: renaming either would break every token and
every client that named it, so neither is renamed inside a version.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

X-Correlation-Id.description: The id that ties this request to the rest of the same piece of work. Send the same value on every call in a chain and one search finds all of them; send none and this request's own id is used.

X-RateLimit-Limit.description: How many requests this allowance is, in the window it counts over. It is the tighter of the limits that apply to you; which one that is is not said.

X-RateLimit-Remaining.description: How many requests are left in that allowance, this one included. At `0` the next request is refused with `429 rate_limited`; slow down before then.

X-RateLimit-Reset.description: How many seconds until the allowance frees a place — seconds from now, the same unit as `Retry-After`, never a timestamp.

X-Request-Id.description: This one request's id — the value you sent, or one minted here if you sent none. Include this id when reporting a problem.

400.description:
**`invalid`** — The input does not hold. The answer names each field that is wrong and why, in the schema's own field names, so the failure can be pointed at rather than guessed at.
- Read the failing fields and resend (`field:errors`)
- Read the shape this endpoint accepts (`docs:openapi`)

**`invalid_cursor`** — That cursor is not one this API issued for this walk. A cursor is opaque and signed, and it names a position in ONE list in ONE ordering — editing one, presenting one to a different list, or replaying one against a different sort order has no meaning to answer. Nothing was skipped and nothing was lost.
- Start the walk again with no cursor (`field:cursor`)
- Follow the next_cursor the last response gave you (`field:next_cursor`)

example.detail: The request could not be completed.

remedies.label: Read the failing fields and resend
Read the shape this endpoint accepts

X-Correlation-Id.description: The id that ties this request to the rest of the same piece of work. Send the same value on every call in a chain and one search finds all of them; send none and this request's own id is used.

get.description:
List the organizations you can see, in tree order.

You get your acting organization — the one the `X-Org` request header names
— and every organization beneath it. Organizations above yours, and those in
other branches, are not returned at all.

Narrow the list with `name` (matches part of a name) or `depth` (an exact
level in the tree). Search names and slugs with `q`. Sort with `ordering`,
which accepts `created_at`, `updated_at`, `name`, `path` or `depth`, each
optionally prefixed with `-` to reverse it; any other value is rejected with
`invalid` and the response lists what you may sort by. Walk it with
`?cursor=` and `?limit=`.

Ask `can` with a permission key — `?can=widget.move` — and the list keeps
only the organizations where you may do that: the destinations a move can
reach, or any other "where may I" question, answered by the same rules a
write is judged by. A key this product does not have is rejected with
`invalid` naming `can`, never answered with an empty list.

The default sort is `path`, which returns the list in tree order — every
organization after the one it hangs from — so you can build a tree from a
single response without a second request.

Returns `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`. Send the
`next_cursor` back as `?cursor=` for the next page and stop when `has_more`
is false; `count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, a
  filter value was malformed, or `?can=` named a permission this product
  does not have. The response names the parameter.
* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — your role here does not let you read organizations. A role
  with no read of this kind reads none of them: ask an administrator for
  the permission, or act under an organization where you hold it.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `org-structure:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `org-structure:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Create an organization under a parent you administer.

Send `parent_id`, `name` and `slug`. There is no way to create an
organization with no parent: every tenant already has exactly one root, made
when the tenant was, and the rest of the tree hangs off it.

`slug` is the handle you will later put in the `X-Org` header to act as this
organization. It must be unique within your tenant; a duplicate answers
`400 invalid` with the clash named in `errors`, and nothing is created.

The parent must be your acting organization or one beneath it, and you must
hold the `admin` or `owner` role over it — held on that organization, or on
any organization above it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed, that `slug` is already
  taken in this tenant, or the tree would go deeper than its limit.
  `errors` names the clash; nothing is created.
* `403 forbidden` — you do not hold `admin` or `owner` over that
  organization, held on it or on one above it. Ask somebody who does.
* `404 not_found` — the `parent_id` is outside the part of the tree you
  can see, or nothing has that id.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `org-structure:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Move an organization, and everything under it, to a new parent.

Send `new_parent_id`. Everything beneath the organization moves with it.

**The move is accepted here and completes shortly afterwards.** The
organization returned by this call is the organization as it stands *now*,
with its old position — re-read it to see the new one. Large subtrees take
longer than small ones.

You must hold `admin` or `owner` over **both** ends: the organization's
current parent and the new parent. Either one you do not administer answers
`forbidden`, and either one outside the part of the tree you can see answers
`not_found`.

Four moves are impossible and answer `invalid`: moving the root, moving
across tenants, moving an organization underneath itself or underneath one
of its own descendants, and any move that would make the tree deeper than
its limit. Asking for a second move of the same organization while the first
is still running is refused rather than queued behind the first.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — the move is one of the four that cannot happen: moving
  the root, moving across tenants, moving an organization under itself
  or under one of its own descendants, or a move that would make the
  tree deeper than its limit.
* `403 forbidden` — you do not hold `admin` or `owner` over BOTH ends —
  the current parent and the new one.
* `404 not_found` — either end is outside the part of the tree you can
  see.
* `409 conflict` — a move of this organization is already running. Wait
  for it to finish; re-read the organization to see where it landed.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `org-structure:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
List the people who belong to the organizations you can see.

Covers your acting organization and everything beneath it. Each entry says
which person (`user_id`, `user_email`), which organization
(`organization_id`) and what role they hold there.

Narrow with `role` or `organization_id`. Sort with `ordering`, which accepts
`created_at`, `updated_at` or `role`, each optionally prefixed with `-`; any
other value is rejected. Walk it with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`.

There is no free-text search on this list. To find one person, filter by
role or organization and walk the list, or fetch the membership by id.

Returns `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`. Send the
`next_cursor` back as `?cursor=` for the next page and stop when `has_more`
is false; `count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — your role here does not let you read memberships. A role
  with no read of this kind reads none of them: ask an administrator for
  the permission, or act under an organization where you hold it.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `roles:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. post.description:
Give a person a role in one of your organizations.

Send `user_id`, `role`, and optionally `organization_id`. **Omit it and the
membership is created on the organization you are acting in** — the one
`X-Org` names, or your default organization when you send no `X-Org`. It is
never created at the top of the tenant on your behalf: a grant is made where
you sent it from. Set `is_default` if this should be the membership used
when the person names no organization.

A role is a set of capability keys; `GET /roles/` lists each role's.

**You cannot hand out what you do not hold.** Every key the role carries
must already be yours at the organization the membership lands on, and
nobody can grant a role in a part of the tree they hold no role over. Both
answer `forbidden`, and the message says which: that you hold no role
there, or the sentences of the keys you are short of.

A `user_id` that matches nobody answers `not_found`, and so does an
`organization_id` outside the part of the tree you can see.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed, or `role` is not one
  this product knows. `errors` names the fields.
* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer that organization, or the `role`
  you asked for is higher than your own there. Nobody grants above
  themselves.
* `404 not_found` — the person or the organization is outside the part of
  the tree you can see, or nothing has that id.
* `409 conflict` — that person already holds a membership on that
  organization. Change the role instead.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

patch.description:
Change the role someone holds.

Send `role` — the key of a role this product knows (`GET /roles/`).

The same ceiling applies as when granting a role in the first place: you
cannot set a role carrying a key you do not hold yourself at that organization,
and you cannot change a membership in a part of the tree you hold no role
over. Both answer `forbidden`.

Demoting the tenant's last `owner` is refused too: a tenant with no owner
is a tenant nobody can administer.

A membership outside the organizations you can see answers `not_found`,
which is also the answer for an id that matches nothing.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `role` is not one this product knows.
* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer that organization, or the new
  role carries a key you do not hold there, or the person already holds a
  key there that you do not.
* `404 not_found` — that membership is outside the part of the tree you
  can see, or nothing has that id.
* `409 conflict` — it is the last `owner` membership in the tenant.
  Promote somebody else first.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `roles:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

delete.description:
Remove a person's membership.

Answers `204` with no body: there is no membership left to return.

Any WebSocket connections that person has open are closed as part of this,
so access ends immediately rather than when they next reload.

You must hold `admin` or `owner` over the organization the membership sits
on, and you cannot remove somebody holding a key there that you do not — both answer
refused. Removing the tenant's last `owner` is refused too: a tenant
with no owner is a tenant nobody can administer.

* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer that organization, or the
  person holds a key there that you do not.

  can see, or nothing has that id.
* `409 conflict` — it is the last `owner` membership in the tenant. Make
  somebody else an owner first.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

- Follow the next_cursor the last response gave you (`field:next_cursor`)

get.description:
List every role this tenant can name, from all three layers at once.

`kind` says which layer a role comes from and decides what you may do with
it. `owner` is the platform's one role: it holds every permission this
deployment declares, present and future, and nothing can change it.
`declared` is a role this product ships in code — you may adjust what it
holds here, not what it is called. `custom` is a role this tenant made for
itself, and both halves are yours.

`permissions` is what the role actually does **in this tenant**;
`default_permissions` is what the product declared it does, and
`added`/`removed` are the difference. For a custom role there is no code
layer, so `default_permissions` is `null`.

Narrow with `kind` or `q` (matches part of the key, name or description).
Sort with `ordering`, which accepts `key`, `name` or `created_at`, each
optionally prefixed with `-`; any other value is rejected. Walk it with
`?cursor=` and `?limit=`.

Returns `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`; `count` is
`null` unless you send `?include_count=true`.

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept. The
  response says what you may sort by.

  not let you read roles.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry `roles:read`.

A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. post.description:

`permissions` takes keys from `GET /permissions/` and also accepts patterns:
`"*.read"` is how you give a role every read this deployment has, and it is
expanded to real keys when the role is saved, so the role does not silently
gain permissions as the product grows. A pattern that matches nothing is
rejected rather than stored.

than the keys. `owner` and any role this product declares in code are taken
names and are rejected.

first answer instead of making a second role.

* `400 invalid` — the key is already a role this product declares, a
  permission is not one this deployment has, or a pattern matched nothing.
  `errors` names the field.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not create roles here, or the collection
  contains something you do not hold.
* `409 conflict` — this tenant already has a role with that key.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished.

get.description:
Read one role by its key, from whichever layer owns it.

The same shape the list returns. A key this tenant cannot name answers
`not_found` — there is no subtree to be outside of, because a role is
tenant-wide rather than held on a branch.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant, or your role here does
  not let you read roles.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry `roles:read`.
* `404 not_found` — nothing in this tenant has that key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `roles:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `roles:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

patch.description:

A membership, a pending invitation and every permission row join on the key,
so it is the immutable half: rename the label and nothing else has to be
rewritten. To change what the role *does*, send its whole collection to

delete.description:
Remove a role this tenant made. Answers `204` with no body.

**Refused while anybody still wears it** — a membership or a pending
invitation naming the key — because the key is a string rather than a
foreign key, so nothing in the database would stop the row disappearing and
the people holding it would quietly hold nothing. Move them to another role
first; the refusal says how many there are.

`owner` and the roles this product declares in code live in code and cannot
be deleted here.

* `403 forbidden` — you may not delete roles here.
* `404 not_found` — this tenant made no role with that key; `owner` and

  offers it.

put.description:
Say what this role may do, as the whole set rather than a list of changes.

Send the collection you want and the server works out the difference, which
is what makes a retry safe. For a role this product declares in code the
difference is stored as a delta, so the role keeps growing with the product:
a permission the next release adds to `member` arrives for you too, unless
you took it away here.

Patterns work exactly as they do on create — `"*.read"` expands to the reads
this deployment has, at the moment you save.

**Both directions are walled.** You cannot add a permission you do not hold
yourself, and you cannot take one away from a role if the people holding it
have something you do not. `owner` is the whole vocabulary by definition and
is rejected: withhold a key from one person instead.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `owner` cannot be edited, a permission is not one this
  deployment has, or a pattern matched nothing.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not change roles here, or the change adds or
  removes something you do not hold.
* `404 not_found` — nothing in this tenant has that key.
* `409 conflict` — the change would leave the tenant with no owner.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

get.description:
List the permissions granted to, or withheld from, one person in one branch.

A grant is what you reach for when a role is the wrong size for one person:
`allow` gives them something their role does not carry, `withhold` takes
away something it does. **A withhold beats everything**, including the
`owner` role, which is why it is the one that needs watching.

Grants hang off the membership rather than the person, so the same person
can carry different exceptions in the branch they run and the branch they
merely belong to.

A membership outside the organizations you can see answers `not_found`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization, or your role here does not let you read grants.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry `roles:read`.
* `404 not_found` — that membership is outside the part of the tree you can
  see, or nothing has that id.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `roles:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `roles:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

put.description:

The membership and the permission are in the path and the body says only
which way the exception points, so sending the same request twice leaves one
row with the last effect on it rather than two rows or a conflict.

you do not have. **`withhold` is bounded by what THEY hold**: you cannot
restrict somebody who has something you do not — otherwise the ceiling would
be decorative, because taking away is the other road to the same power.

either direction.

  reserved.

delete.description:
Withdraw a grant, leaving the person with whatever their role says. `204`.

Removing an `allow` takes a capability away, so it is bounded by what the
person holds; removing a `withhold` gives one back, so it is bounded by what
you hold. The wall that applies depends on which way the row pointed, which
is why `effect` is on the row rather than in the request.

A permission that has no grant on that membership answers `not_found`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you may not remove grants here, or the permission is not
  yours to restore or to take away.
* `404 not_found` — that membership is outside the part of the tree you can
  see, or there is no such grant on it.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `roles:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
Everything this membership may do at its own branch, and where each one
came from.

This is the read a permissions screen is built on: `held` carries every
permission with the sentence a person reads and a `via` saying whether it
comes from the role on this membership, a grant on it, or a role held
further up the tree. When `via` is `inherited`, `membership_id` names the
ancestor membership that carries it rather than this one.

`withheld` is kept separately rather than quietly subtracted, because a
withhold is a decision somebody made and "why has this stopped working" is
a question this answer should be able to settle.

A membership outside the organizations you can see answers `not_found`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization, or your role here does not let you read memberships.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry `roles:read`.
* `404 not_found` — that membership is outside the part of the tree you can
  see, or nothing has that id.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `roles:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

- Follow the next_cursor the last response gave you (`field:next_cursor`)

get.description:
List every permission this deployment has, which is what a role's collection
is chosen from.

A key reads `<kind>.<verb>` — the kind is the thing (`widget`, `membership`)
and the verb is what you do to it. Most are **derived**: the product has a
`widget`, so `widget.create/read/update/delete` exist without anybody typing
them. Some are **declared**, where an app named a verb of its own
(`widget.approve`). One is **reserved** to the `owner` role and no role or
grant may name it.

`sentence` is what a refused caller is told; `default_roles` says which
roles this product gives the key to out of the box; `has_row_predicate`
warns you that holding the key is not the whole answer — the product also
asks about the row, so granting it grants the capability rather than the
outcome.

Narrow with `kind`, `verb`, `decided_by`, `is_read` or `q`. Walk it with
`?cursor=` and `?limit=`; `count` is `null` unless you send
`?include_count=true`.

This list is generated from the running system and is the same for every
customer: it describes what the product can authorize, not what you happen
to have granted.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant, or your role here does
  not let you read roles.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry `roles:read`.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

get.description:
List the invitations issued inside the part of the tree you are acting in.

Each entry says who was invited, **into which organization**, as what role,
how the invitation stands (`pending`, `accepted` or `revoked`), when it
expires and, if it was taken up, when.

**`X-Org` narrows this list.** An invitation records the organization it was
sent from, and you see the ones at or below your acting organization —
so a branch manager sees their own branch's offers and not the branch beside
them. Send `X-Org` naming a node you belong to, or omit it and act in your
default organization.

Narrow with `status`, `email` or `organization_id`. Search addresses with
`q`. Sort with
`ordering`, which accepts `created_at`, `updated_at`, `email` or
`expires_at`, each optionally prefixed with `-`; any other value answers
`invalid`. Walk it with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`.

**Invitation tokens are never on this response.** A pending invitation's
token is a credential — whoever holds it becomes a member — so it is
returned only once, by the call that issues it. If you have lost one, issue
a new invitation; nothing will show you the old one again.

Returns `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`. Send the
`next_cursor` back as `?cursor=` for the next page and stop when `has_more`
is false; `count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant` naming
  one you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — your role here does not let you read invitations. A role
  with no read of this kind reads none of them: ask an administrator for
  the permission, or act under an organization where you hold it.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `invitations:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `invitations:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org

It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. post.description:
Invite a person into one of your organizations. Returns the invitation and
its token.

Send `email` and, optionally, `role` (defaults to `member`) and
`organization_id`.

**Omit `organization_id` and the invitation is placed in the organization
you are acting in** — the one `X-Org` names, or your default organization
when you send no `X-Org`. It is never placed at the top of the tenant on
your behalf: an invitation sent from a branch is an offer of a place in that
branch, and when the person accepts, that is exactly where their membership
lands. Name an `organization_id` to place it somewhere else inside the part
of the tree you can see; a node outside that answers `not_found`.

**The `token` in the response is the only copy that will ever exist.** Only
a hash of it is stored, so nothing here can show it to you again. Put it in
the link you send the invitee. If you lose it, issue a new invitation.

An invitation email is also sent for you.

Inviting somebody who already has a pending invitation **in the same
organization** replaces that invitation rather than failing — the older one
is withdrawn and the new token is the one that works. An invitation standing
in a different organization is untouched: two branches may each have a live
offer out to the same person, because they are offers of two places.

Two separate permissions apply and both answer `forbidden`, and **both are
asked about the organization the invitation is placed in**: you must hold
`admin` or `owner` there to invite anybody at all, and you cannot invite
somebody at a role carrying a key you do not hold there.

post.description:
Redeem an invitation token and become a member of the tenant that sent it.

Send the `token` from the invitation link, and nothing else. **Nothing in
the request says who is accepting** — whoever your credential identifies
becomes the member, and there is no way to accept on somebody else's behalf.
So the person joining has to be signed in themselves, whether that is a
browser session or their own bearer token.

You do not need to be a member of the tenant that invited you; that is the
point. The invitation is looked up across the whole product by its token.

**You land exactly where the invitation was sent from.** An invitation
records the organization it was issued in, and that is the organization your
membership is created on — not the top of the tenant. Nothing in this
request can change it: the placement was decided by the person who invited
you, bounded by what they themselves could reach.

Returns the membership that was created — the person, the organization and
the role the invitation named.

**This capability is not available as an MCP tool**, and it is the only one
that is not: accepting is the moment a person joins, and an agent acting for
somebody who has not joined yet has nobody to act for.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — nobody is signed in. Sign the person in, then retry.
* `404 not_found` — that token matches no invitation waiting to be accepted.
* `409 conflict` — the invitation has already been accepted, or was
  withdrawn.
* `400 invalid` — the invitation has expired. Ask for a new one.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

delete.description:
Withdraw an invitation, so its token stops working.

Answers with the invitation itself rather than an empty body: it is still
listed after this, with `status` moved to `revoked`, and seeing the new
status is more useful than seeing nothing.

Withdrawing an invitation that is already withdrawn succeeds and changes
nothing, so a retry after a timeout is safe.

**You must hold `admin` or `owner` over the organization the invitation was
sent from** — the one it will place its person in. An invitation issued
outside the part of the tree you are acting in is not visible here at all,
and answers `not_found` rather than `forbidden`, as does one belonging to
another tenant.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  organization this invitation is placed in.
* `404 not_found` — no invitation you can see has that id.
* `409 conflict` — it has already been accepted, so there is nothing left
  to withdraw.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `invitations:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

put.description:
Change this tenant's configuration.

Send any of `values`, `timezone` and `locale`; anything you leave out is
left alone.

**`values` is merged, not replaced.** Send one key and one key changes;
every other key in `settings` survives. To remove a key, send it with the
value `null`.

`timezone` must be a name from the IANA time zone database, such as
`Europe/Lisbon`. Anything else is refused rather than being stored
and failing later when a date is rendered.

You must hold `admin` or `owner` over the tenant as a whole — not merely
over the organization you are acting as.
Configuration applies to everybody in the tenant, so administering one
branch of it is not enough.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a value is outside what the setting accepts. `errors`
  names the fields and nothing is changed.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant, or the request resolved no tenant.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an

post.description:
Erase your own account. **This cannot be undone by anybody.**

Send no body. Your email address is replaced with an unreachable
`erased+<random>@erased.invalid` address, your password is made unusable,
every API token you hold is revoked for good, any admin access you had is
removed, your open WebSocket connections are closed, and your account with
the identity provider you sign in through is switched off. You cannot sign
in again, and neither can anybody acting as you.

Your account record and your tenant memberships are kept. That is
deliberate: records elsewhere that say who did something — who approved a
refund, who changed a setting — have to keep reading correctly, and deleting
the account would turn every one of them into a dangling reference. The
account cannot be used regardless.

confirmation that the erasure happened.

  would leave it with nobody who can administer it. The message names each
  tenant. Make somebody else an owner there first, then retry.

  Send `X-Tenant` naming one you belong to.

post.description:
Switch someone's account off. This can be undone.

Send no body; `user_id` in the path is the person. The same thing happens to
them as when they switch their own account off: their browser session ends,
their API tokens start answering `401` without being revoked, and their open
WebSocket connections are closed. Nothing is deleted and their email address
is unchanged, so the change can be reversed by switching the account back on.

**Who may call this:** you, over your own account, or an administrator or
owner of the whole tenant you are signed in to. Administrators of one
part of a larger tenant cannot switch off people in another part —
switching an account off affects the person everywhere, so it takes
tenant-wide authority.

  tenant, send `X-Tenant` naming that one.
* `403 forbidden` — the person is in your tenant, but you are neither
  them nor an administrator of the whole tenant. Ask an owner or
  administrator to do it.

post.description:
Erase someone's account. **This cannot be undone by anybody.**

Send no body; `user_id` in the path is the person. Their email address is
replaced with an unreachable `erased+<random>@erased.invalid` address, their
password is made unusable, every API token they hold is revoked for good,
any admin access is removed, their open WebSocket connections are closed,
and their account with the identity provider is switched off. Neither they
nor anybody acting as them can sign in again.

Their account record and tenant memberships are kept, so records
elsewhere that say who did something keep reading correctly. The account
cannot be used regardless.

**Who may call this:** you, over your own account, or an administrator or
owner of the whole tenant you are signed in to. Administrators of one
part of a larger tenant cannot erase people in another part — an erasure
reaches the person in every tenant they belong to and with the identity
provider as well, so it takes tenant-wide authority.

your confirmation that the erasure happened.

* `409 conflict` — the person is the only owner of a tenant, and erasing
  them would leave it with nobody who can administer it. The message names
  each tenant. Make somebody else an owner there first, then retry.
* `404 not_found` — nobody with that id belongs to the tenant you are
  signed in to. You get this whether or not such an account exists anywhere,
  so it is not a way to check.
* `403 forbidden` — the person is in your tenant, but you are neither
  them nor an administrator of the whole tenant.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

post.description:
Create a bearer token for yourself, so a program can call this API as you.

**You must be signed in with a browser session to call this, and the request
needs a CSRF token** — send the `csrftoken` cookie's value in the
`X-CSRFToken` header, as you would for any other session-authenticated
write. A bearer token cannot mint another bearer token: a token that could
would survive being revoked, because its offspring would keep working.

**So no token reaches this, and no scope changes that.** A bearer token here
is refused `session_required` — before anything looks at what the token
carries, because looking would produce the wrong answer: "your token needs a
wider scope" would be true of no token at all, and the wider token would
have to be minted here, by a token, which is the thing that is refused. If
you are holding a token and you need another one, there are two doors that
mint and neither of them is this one from where you are standing: a
signed-in browser session, and the shell command on a machine that runs this
deployment.

Send a `name` — anything you will recognise later in a list of tokens, such
as `"nightly export"` — and `scopes`, which says what the token is allowed
to reach.

**`scopes` has no default and leaving it out is refused.** A token you are
about to paste into somebody else's software should be as narrow as the job
needs, and a default would quietly make it as wide as you are. Send a list
of names, each one a section of this API followed by `:read` or `:write` —
`"widgets:read"`, `"tenant-settings:write"`. The sections are the headings
this reference page groups operations under, and every operation says which
scope it needs in its own description; `/llms.txt` lists the whole
vocabulary in one place. Two forms are refused rather than guessed at: an
empty list (a token that can do nothing is a mistake, not a narrow one),
and a name this deployment does not have. If the token really should be
able to do everything you can, say so out loud: send `["*"]`.

**Within a section, the write scope includes the read.** Asking for
`"widgets:write"` gets you reading widgets as well, so you do not have to
remember the pair — and `effective_scopes` in the response shows you both,
so what the token can do is on the screen rather than in your head. It
works one way only, and never across sections: a read scope never allows a
write, and `"widgets:write"` says nothing at all about any other section.

The response tells you two things about what you asked for. `scopes` is
what the token carries — `null` when you sent `["*"]`, meaning no limit.
`effective_scopes` is the part of it your own role can back today, so a
scope you asked for that is missing from that list is one the role
underneath will refuse anyway, and you find that out here rather than in a
log six hours later.

A scope only ever narrows. It cannot grant: your role and the rules on each
record still decide, so a token scoped to a section you are not allowed to
write to is refused exactly as you would be.

**The token is in the response, once.** Nothing reads it back: there is no
route that returns it, and it is stored only as a hash, so if you lose it
you mint another and revoke this one. Send it on later requests as
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

The token is pinned to the tenant you are acting in when you mint it — the
one `X-Tenant` names, or your default. It can only ever act in that tenant.
A later request that sends no `X-Tenant` acts in the pin, which is the
ordinary way to use it; a later request that sends `X-Tenant` naming a
*different* tenant is refused with `403 addressing_header_not_honoured`,
never quietly answered as the pin — the token authenticated, and what was
refused is where it asked to act.

Returns `201` with the token's `id`, `name`, `tenant_id`, `created_at`,
`scopes`, `effective_scopes` and the `token` itself. `last_used_at` and
`revoked_at` are `null` on a token this new.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 session_required` — you called with a bearer token instead of a
  browser session. No token can make this call, so there is no wider one to
  go and mint; sign in, or ask somebody with a shell on the server.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — you are signed in, and the request resolved no tenant.
  Send `X-Tenant` naming a tenant you belong to.
* `400 invalid` — the `name` was empty or longer than 200 characters, or
  `scopes` was missing, empty, or named something this API does not have.
  `errors` says which.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** none — **no bearer token reaches this call**, whatever scopes it carries, so there is no token to mint and none to widen. A token that tries is refused `session_required`. Sign in with a browser session and make the call from there.

delete.description:
Stop one of your own API tokens working, immediately and permanently.

`token_id` in the path is the token. You can only revoke your own: a token
belonging to anybody else answers `404`, whether or not it exists.

It takes effect at once: the next request carrying that token answers `401`.
Every WebSocket connection you currently have open is closed as well — all
of them, not only the ones this token opened, because a connection that was
already authenticated would otherwise keep receiving until the client hung
up. Reconnect with a credential that still works. There is no route that
un-revokes a token; mint a new one.

The token's record is kept, so anything it did is still attributable
afterwards. Nothing about it can be read back, and the secret never could
be.

Send no body. Answers `204` with an empty body.

You may call this with the token you are revoking. That is deliberate: a
program that discovers its own credential has leaked can disable it without
finding a person, and doing so reaches nothing else.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no token of yours has that id.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `tokens:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Ask where an email address should be sent to sign in, before anybody is
signed in.

**This route takes no credential** — a login form has to answer this
question before it has one. Send `{"email": "..."}` and you get back:

* `authorize_url` — where to send the person's browser. Always present.
* `method` — always `sso`; every sign-in goes through the same provider.
* `connection_id` — present only when the address's domain belongs to an
  identity provider one of our customers has configured, in which case
  `authorize_url` already carries a hint that skips the provider chooser.

The answer deliberately tells you nothing else. An address whose domain
nobody has claimed, an address whose provider has been switched off, and an
address nobody has ever heard of all get the same reply, so this cannot be
used to discover which companies use this product.

It is rate-limited per calling address more tightly than the rest of the
API, for the same reason.

* `400 invalid` — the `email` was missing, empty or longer than 320
  characters.

  seconds and try again.

get.description:
List the identity providers configured for the tenant you are acting in.

An identity provider is what lets a company sign its own people in to this
product with their own login. This is the tenant's list of them, newest
first by default; `?ordering=` accepts `created_at`, `updated_at`, `name` or
`status`, each with `-` in front of it for descending.

Paginated with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`:
`{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, and `count` only
when you send `?include_count=true`.

**No client secret is ever in a response**, from this route or any other.
Each entry carries `has_client_secret` so you can see that one is stored
without seeing it.

`status` is `active` or `disabled`; a disabled provider signs nobody in but
keeps its record and its claim on its email domains.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. post.description:
Configure an OpenID Connect provider so a tenant's people can sign in with
their own company login.

**Only an owner or an administrator of the tenant may call this.** It is the
strictest permission in this API: whoever configures a provider decides who
may become a member of the tenant and at what role.

Send the provider's `issuer` URL, its `client_id` and `client_secret`, a
`name` you will recognise, and `email_domains` — the domains this provider
owns, such as `acme.com`. Optionally `default_role` (the role key people who
arrive through it join at; the deployment's default role unless you say
otherwise, and it never changes an existing membership) and `enforced` (when
`true`, people in those domains may not sign in any other way).

**An email domain belongs to exactly one provider across the whole
product.** Claiming one somebody else already has is refused.

**Claiming a domain reserves it; it does not route anybody yet.** Nobody
signs in through this provider until an operator of this deployment confirms
that your organisation owns the domain — ask them to, and they will tell you
when it is done. Public mail providers such as `gmail.com` are refused here
outright: an identity provider claims the domains its organisation owns.

**`default_role` may not be higher than your own role in the tenant.** A
provider is a grant that happens later, so an administrator cannot configure
one that turns arrivals into owners.

The secret is stored encrypted and no route returns it. The response
reports `has_client_secret: true` instead.

Returns `201` with the provider. `protocol` is `oidc`; nothing else is
accepted. `verified_domains` is empty until an operator verifies, and it is
the list that says which of your `email_domains` route a sign-in today.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or administrator of this tenant.
  **Measured at the tenant's root**: an administrator of one branch
  administers that branch, and may not configure the tenant's identity
  provider.
* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed, or `protocol` was
  anything but `oidc`. `errors` names the fields.
* `409 conflict` — one of the `email_domains` is already claimed.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `auth:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org

It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat.
