patch.description:
Change the settings of one identity provider this tenant has configured.

`connection_id` in the path is the provider. **Owner or administrator of the
tenant only**, like creating one.

Send only the fields you are changing — `name`, `issuer`, `client_id`,
`client_secret`, `email_domains`, `default_role`, `enforced`. Anything you
leave out is left alone, and **leaving out `client_secret` keeps the stored
one**: it is the only thing omitting it can mean, since nothing can read it
back to re-send it.

Sending `email_domains` **replaces** the list rather than adding to it, and
the same one-domain-one-provider rule applies. A domain you keep keeps its
verification; one you remove and send again later starts unverified, and an
operator has to confirm it before it routes anybody again.

Returns the provider as it now is. No secret is ever in the response.
`verified_domains` says which of the claims route today.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no provider with that id belongs to the tenant you are
  acting in.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or administrator of this tenant.
  **Measured at the tenant's root**: an administrator of one branch
  administers that branch, and may not configure the tenant's identity
  provider.
* `400 invalid` — a field you sent is malformed, or `default_role` is above
  your own role. `errors` names the fields.
* `409 conflict` — one of the `email_domains` is already claimed elsewhere.
* `409 enforced_without_provider` — you switched `enforced` on before this
  provider was set up at the identity platform; requiring it now would leave
  its people no way to sign in. Read the provider back until `sync_state` is
  `applied`, then switch it on.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

`enforced` in the answer is what the identity platform has applied, not only
what you asked for: it reads `false` with `sync_state` `pending` until the

tenant only.** Send no body; answers `204` with an empty body.

get.description:
List messages your acting organization has sent, newest first.

Narrow with `status`, `channel` or `template` (each an exact match; the
template one matches the template's name). Sort with `ordering`, which
accepts `created_at`, `updated_at`, `sent_at` or `status`, each optionally
prefixed with `-`; the default is `-created_at` and any other value is
refused with `400 invalid`. Paged with `?cursor=` and `?limit=` (50 by
default, 200 at most); the body is
`{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}` — follow
`next_cursor` while `has_more` is true. `count` is `null` unless you ask
with `?include_count=true`.

**Messages that were never sent are in this list too.** A message the
product refused to deliver — because consent was withdrawn, quiet hours were
in force, or the address was suppressed — is here with
`status: "suppressed"` and a `suppressed_reason`. That is the point of the
list: "why did they not get the email" is answered here, and would not be if
the refusals were hidden.

Which messages you see depends on the organization you are acting as (the
`X-Org` header) — its own and those of organizations beneath it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow you to read this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `messaging:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Send one message to one contact.

Send `recipient_id`, then **one** of two things:

* a `template` name, optionally with `channel` (defaults to `email`) — one
  message, once; or
* a `policy` name — an escalation the product runs for you, whose own first
  step already decides the template and the channel.

Sending `template` or `channel` **alongside** `policy` is refused with
`400 invalid` naming the offending field, rather than resolved one way.

`template` is a name, not an id: ask for `"invoice-reminder"` and the latest
live version of it is used. There is no way to pin an older one.

`context` is the object of variables the template fills in. It is checked
against that template's declared shape first, so a missing or wrong-typed
variable is a `400 invalid` naming the field and **nothing is sent**.

**`send_at` schedules it.** Give a timezone-aware moment and the answer is
`201` with `status: "queued"` immediately, while the message itself waits.
Three things are worth knowing before you rely on it:

* consent is checked **twice** — now, and again the moment it goes out. A
  send scheduled for next week to somebody who unsubscribes on Tuesday does
  not go. Scheduling is not a way to bank permission;
* a moment **already past** sends now. It is not an error, because your
  clock and ours disagreeing by a second must not be one;
* a moment with **no timezone** is refused with `400 invalid`. There is no
  default zone and there will not be one: a scheduled send is a promise
  about an instant, and guessing whose midnight you meant is the one
  mistake that cannot be recovered from afterwards.

There is no way to cancel or re-schedule one yet, and no list of what is
pending — a scheduled message reads as `queued` like any other. Both are
named gaps rather than oversights.

**`201` does not mean the message went out.** Read `status` on the answer:

* `queued` — accepted, and delivery has started. Poll
  `GET /api/v1/messages/{message_id}/` for where it got to.
* `suppressed` — nothing was sent. `suppressed_reason` says why:
  `suppressed` (this address is blocked on this channel and even
  transactional mail stops), `no_consent` (this is a marketing message and
  nobody has agreed to it on this channel), or `quiet_hours` (a marketing
  message inside the person's quiet window — it is dropped, not delayed).
  The consent routes under `/recipients/{recipient_id}/` are where each of
  those is changed. If you sent a `policy` with more than one step, its
  later steps still run; each is consent-checked again at its own send time.

Both are `201`, because both are the product working correctly. A client
that treats any 2xx as "delivered" will be wrong; read the row.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — you sent `template` or `channel` alongside `policy`,
  sent neither, named a template or policy that has no live version, the
  `context` did not match the template's declared variables, or `send_at`
  carried no timezone. `errors` names the field and nothing is sent.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
Fetch one message by id, and where its delivery has got to.

This is how you follow a `queued` message: `status` moves on after the send
returned, so poll here rather than trusting the answer you got at send time.
`sent_at`, `delivered_at` and `bounced_at` are filled in as each happens, and
`error` and `bounce_kind` say what went wrong when something did.

The row is a record of what was **attempted**. Even `delivered` is the
provider's word for it, not proof anybody read it.

A message your acting organization cannot see, or an id that names nothing,
answers `404 not_found`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no message your acting organization can see has that
  id.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow you to read this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `messaging:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

400.description:
**`invalid_cursor`** — That cursor is not one this API issued for this walk. A cursor is opaque and signed, and it names a position in ONE list in ONE ordering — editing one, presenting one to a different list, or replaying one against a different sort order has no meaning to answer. Nothing was skipped and nothing was lost.

- Follow the next_cursor the last response gave you (`field:next_cursor`)

**`invalid`** — The input does not hold. The answer names each field that is wrong and why, in the schema's own field names, so the failure can be pointed at rather than guessed at.
- Read the failing fields and resend (`field:errors`)
- Read the shape this endpoint accepts (`docs:openapi`)

get.description:
List the opens and clicks a provider has reported for one message.

**These are a provider's inferences, not facts about delivery.** An open is
recorded when something requested the tracking image in the message, and on
Apple Mail Privacy Protection that request is made for every message a
person receives whether they look at it or not — so a message can show opens
nobody made. A click is stronger, because a person's own action caused it.
Neither says the message arrived: `GET /api/v1/messages/{message_id}/` is
where delivery lives, and nothing on this list moves it.

Newest first by when the *provider* says it happened, which is not when we
heard: `occurred_at` is the provider's moment and `created_at` is ours, and
a webhook that arrived an hour late does not sort as an hour-late open. Sort
with `ordering`, which accepts `occurred_at` or `created_at`, each
optionally prefixed with `-`. Paged with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`; `count`
is `null` unless you ask with `?include_count=true`.

`kind` is `opened` or `clicked` and there is no third value. A spam
complaint is deliberately not here: it is news about consent, it suppresses
the address, and it arrives as the `comms.message.complained` event. `url`
is the link on a click and is empty on an open.

**There is no way to add a row through this API, on purpose.** An engagement
is something a transport told us about a person, and a door that accepted
one would let a client mint "opened" facts about somebody else into a record
whose whole value is that it was witnessed. The only writer is the
signature-verified provider webhook.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow you to read this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `404 not_found` — no message your acting organization can see has that
  id, or `?cursor=` did not come from this list.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `messaging:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

409.description:
**`conflict`** — Something that already exists holds the name, the identifier or the state this write asked for. Nothing was written.
- Re-read the row and retry against what is true now (`self:reread`)
- Ask for the first answer back instead of a second attempt (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`idempotency_key_reuse`** — This Idempotency-Key has already been used, for a different request. The fingerprint covers the method, the path and the body, so one changed byte is a different request under a key that is already spoken for. Nothing was written.
- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

post.description:
Take a message back out of the queue, before anything has been sent.

Send no body. Use it for a scheduled send you have changed your mind about —
`send_at` on the message tells you whether there is still time.

**Only a message that is still `queued` can be cancelled**, and that is the
whole safety of it. Once `status` reaches `sending` a transport has it in
hand at that moment, and anything past that has already happened to
somebody. Those all answer `409 conflict` naming the status, rather than
quietly doing nothing — a caller who believes a sent message was stopped is
worse off than one who is told.

The answer is the message with `status: "cancelled"`. That is its own
status and not a suppression: `suppressed` is this product refusing on the
**recipient's** behalf — they opted out, they were suppressed, it was their
quiet hours — and counting a sender's change of mind among those would put
an opt-out in your reports that nobody made.

**Cancelling twice is a `409`, not a shrug.** The first one settled it;
the second is a caller who believes something that is not true.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no message your acting organization can see has that
  id. A message in a branch you hold no membership over answers this too.
* `409 conflict` — that message is past the point of being cancelled. The
  detail names the status it is in.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

get.description:
List message templates — **every version, including retired ones.**

A template name has many versions and this returns all of them, so expect
several rows sharing one `name` with different `version` numbers. `is_active`
marks the one a send under that name would use right now. Retired versions
stay in the list because a message sent in March records the version it went
out with, and you need to be able to read those exact words back.

Narrow with `name`, `channel` or `category` (each exact). Sort with
`ordering`, which accepts `name`, `version`, `created_at` or `updated_at`,
each optionally prefixed with `-`; the default is `name` and any other value
is refused with `400 invalid`. Paged with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`; the
body is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, and
`count` arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

Templates belong to the whole tenant, not to one organization within it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow you to read this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `messaging:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

409.description:
**`conflict`** — Something that already exists holds the name, the identifier or the state this write asked for. Nothing was written.
- Re-read the row and retry against what is true now (`self:reread`)
- Ask for the first answer back instead of a second attempt (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`idempotency_key_reuse`** — This Idempotency-Key has already been used, for a different request. The fingerprint covers the method, the path and the body, so one changed byte is a different request under a key that is already spoken for. Nothing was written.
- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

post.description:
Create a new template at version 1.

Send `name` (how you will refer to it when sending) and `body` (the text,
with `{{ variable }}` placeholders). Optionally `subject`, `channel`
(defaults to `email`), `category` (`transactional` or `marketing` — this is
what decides whether consent and quiet hours can stop a send), and
`context_schema`, an object declaring the variables the body expects so that
a send with the wrong ones is refused rather than delivered half-filled.

post.description:
Publish the next version of a template.

Put the template's `name` in the path and the new `body` in the body, plus
optionally `subject`, `category` and `context_schema`.

`category` and `context_schema` carry over from the current version when you
omit them. **`subject` does not** — omit it and the new version has an empty
subject, so send it every time even when it is unchanged.

**This does not edit anything.** You get `201` and a *new* template — a new
`id`, at `version + 1` — and every earlier version stays exactly as it was.
That is deliberate: messages already sent record the version they went out
with, and rewriting one would change the record of what somebody was told.
There is no route anywhere in this API that edits a template.

**The channel cannot change across versions** and there is no field here to
change it: an email template stays an email template for ever, because
moving it would silently re-target every send that names it. Sending on
another channel means a new template with a new name.

New sends under this name start using the new version immediately. An
escalation already running keeps the version it started with.

A `name` this tenant does not have answers `404 not_found`. Requires an
owner or admin role.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed. `errors` names the
  fields and no version is published.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no template of this tenant's has that name.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

post.description:
Retire the live version of a template, by name.

Takes no body. Put the template's `name` in the path — the same name you
revise with and the same name you send with. It retires whichever version is
currently live under that name: `is_active` becomes false and sends stop
choosing it, but the name keeps working and now resolves to the highest
version still active, so retiring v3 puts v2 back into service. Retiring the
only version leaves the name with nothing to resolve to, and a send naming
it fails.

Nothing is deleted. Every retired version stays readable through
`GET /api/v1/templates/?name=<name>`, and every message that used one still
records the name and version it went out with.

**Safe to retry** under an `Idempotency-Key`: the replay answers with the
first call's result rather than retiring a second version. Without a key,
a second call is a second retirement — it takes out whatever is live now.

A `name` this tenant does not have, or one whose every version is already
retired, answers `404 not_found`. Owner or administrator of the tenant only.
Answers `200` with the template.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no template of this tenant's has that name, or it has
  no live version to retire.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
List delivery policies — **every version, including retired ones.**

A delivery policy is an escalation plan: an ordered list of `steps` the
product works through when you name the policy on a send instead of a
template. Each step says which `channel` to try, which `template` to use,
how many `wait_seconds` to wait for the provider to report back, and
`escalate_when` — `"delivered"` to try the next step if this one was not
delivered, `"none"` to stop here. A step that is delivered always ends the
chain, whatever the plan said next.

Like templates, a policy name has many versions and all of them are here, so
expect several rows sharing one `name`. `is_active` marks the one a send
under that name would run now. Retired versions stay because a message
records the policy name and version it ran under, and reading back what an
escalation actually did in March needs the steps as they were then.

Narrow with `name` (exact). Sort with `ordering`, which accepts `name`,
`version`, `created_at` or `updated_at`, each optionally prefixed with `-`;
the default is `name`, with the newest version of each name first, and any
other value is refused with `400 invalid`. Paged with `?cursor=` and
`?limit=`; the body is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`,
and `count` arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

Policies belong to the whole tenant, not to one organization within it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow you to read this.

post.description:
Create a new delivery policy at version 1.

Send `name` and `steps` — at least one, in the order they should be tried.
Each step needs `channel` and `template`, and takes `wait_seconds` (default
0, meaning move on without waiting for a provider status) and
`escalate_when`, which is `"delivered"` (try the next step if this one was
not delivered) or `"none"` (stop here, the default).

Each step's `template` must already exist **and be on that step's channel**;
a mismatch is `400 invalid` with the offending step and field named, and
nothing is created. So is an `escalate_when` that is neither of the two
values, and so is any field not on this shape.

A `name` this tenant already has answers `409 conflict`. Use
`POST /api/v1/delivery-policies/{name}/versions/` to change one instead.

Owner or administrator of the tenant only. Answers `201` with the new policy.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed, or a step names a
  template or channel this product does not know. `errors` names the
  fields and nothing is created.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `409 conflict` — a policy already exists under that name. Publish a new
  version of it instead.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.

post.description:
Publish the next version of a delivery policy.

Put the policy's `name` in the path and the complete new `steps` list in the
body — steps are replaced wholesale, not merged, so send every step you want
the new version to have.

**This does not edit anything.** You get `201` and a *new* policy at
`version + 1`; earlier versions stay exactly as they were, so what an
escalation did in the past stays readable. There is no route that edits a
policy in place.

**Safe to publish while an escalation is running.** An escalation already
under way — including one part-way through a wait — keeps running the
version it started with; it cannot be changed underneath itself. Sends
started after this call use the new version.

Each step is validated as it is on create: the `template` must exist and be
on that step's `channel`, or you get `400 invalid` naming the step and field
and nothing is created. A `name` this tenant does not have answers
`404 not_found`.

Owner or administrator of the tenant only.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed. `errors` names the
  fields and no version is published.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no policy of this tenant's has that name.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

**`insufficient_scope`** — This token is limited to a set of scopes, and this operation needs one it does not carry. Nothing was read and nothing was written. - Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)
- Check which memberships you actually hold (`self:membership`)

**`no_acting_scope`** — You are who you say you are, and this request resolved no workspace, or no part of one, for you to act in — you hold no membership it could act under. Nothing was read and nothing was written.

- Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)

409.description:
**`conflict`** — Something that already exists holds the name, the identifier or the state this write asked for. Nothing was written.
- Re-read the row and retry against what is true now (`self:reread`)
- Ask for the first answer back instead of a second attempt (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`idempotency_key_reuse`** — This Idempotency-Key has already been used, for a different request. The fingerprint covers the method, the path and the body, so one changed byte is a different request under a key that is already spoken for. Nothing was written.
- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

post.description:
Retire the live version of a policy, by name.

Takes no body. It retires whichever version is currently live under that
name — the name keeps working and now resolves to the highest version still
active, so retiring v3 puts v2 back into service. Retiring the only version
leaves the name with nothing to resolve to, and a send naming it fails.

Escalations already running are untouched: each keeps the plan it started
with. So are the messages that recorded it.

**Safe to retry.** Retiring when the live version is already retired answers
`200` and changes nothing, rather than conflicting.

A `name` this tenant does not have answers `404 not_found`. Requires an
owner or admin role.

* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no policy of this tenant's has that name, or it has no
  live version to retire.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.

List the contacts your acting organization can address.

Narrow with `email` (case-insensitive substring). Sort with `ordering`,
which accepts `email`, `display_name`, `created_at` or `updated_at`, each
optionally prefixed with `-`; the default is `email` and any other value is
refused with `400 invalid`. Paged with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`; the body
is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, and `count`
arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

archived ones and `?show=all` lists both; the default is `?show=live`.

the parameter to ask with instead, rather than ignored.

person may exist as a separate contact in a different part of the tenant,
and you will not see that one.

contact as it stands — and the page carries its own `allowed_acts`, which
holds `create` when you may add a contact where you are acting.

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept,

  parameter and what it accepts.

post.description:
Add a contact your acting organization can address.

Send `email` — it is the contact's identity here and is lower-cased — and
optionally `display_name`, `phone` and `chat_handle`.

A contact is not a user account: they never sign in, and creating one gives
nobody access to anything.

**They arrive having consented to nothing.** Transactional messages will
reach them straight away; anything marketing is refused until you grant
consent per channel with
`POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/grant-consent/`.

The contact is created in the organization you are acting as (the `X-Org`
header), and that is what decides who else in the tenant can see them. There
is no field that names a different one. An email that organization already
holds answers `409 conflict` — but the same email in another part of the
tenant is a separate contact and does not clash.

Answers `201` with the contact.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed. `errors` names the
  fields and nothing is created.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `409 conflict` — this organization already has a contact at that
  address.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

get.description:
Fetch one contact by id.

Archived contacts resolve here even though they are out of the list, so a
message you found in the log can always be traced to who it went to. An
archived contact reads read-only: `archived_at` and `archived_by` say when
and by whom, and every change other than
`POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/restore/` is refused with
`409 archived`.

A contact your acting organization cannot see, or an id that names nothing,
answers `404 not_found`.

`allowed_acts` names the acts you may take on this contact as it stands: an
archived contact offers only `restore`.

Consent is not on this shape. Read it at
`GET /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/preferences/`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow you to read this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `messaging:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

409.description:

- Restore it first (`route:recipient-restore`)

**`conflict`** — Something that already exists holds the name, the identifier or the state this write asked for. Nothing was written.
- Re-read the row and retry against what is true now (`self:reread`)
- Ask for the first answer back instead of a second attempt (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`idempotency_key_reuse`** — This Idempotency-Key has already been used, for a different request. The fingerprint covers the method, the path and the body, so one changed byte is a different request under a key that is already spoken for. Nothing was written.
- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

patch.description:
Correct a contact's details.

Four fields can be changed and no others: `email`, `display_name`, `phone`
and `chat_handle`. Send only the ones you want to change; anything you omit
is left alone.

**A body naming any other field is refused with `400 invalid` and the field
named** — nothing is accepted and silently ignored here, so if this call
succeeds, everything you sent took effect.

In particular you cannot change through this route: whether the contact is
archived (use `POST .../archive/`), which organization holds them, or
anything about their consent, quiet hours or suppression (those are the
routes under `/recipients/{recipient_id}/` named for each verb). Those are
separate operations because each is a decision somebody made at a moment,
recorded as such, rather than a column to be overwritten.

Answers `200` with the contact as it now stands.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field you sent is malformed. `errors` names it and
  nothing is changed.
* `403 forbidden` — your membership here does not allow this.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `409 archived` — the contact is archived and reads read-only. Restore it
  with `POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/restore/` first.
* `409 conflict` — this organization already has a contact at that
  address.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Archive a contact.

Takes no body. The contact drops out of `GET /api/v1/recipients/`
(`?show=archived` lists them again), stays fetchable by id, and stays
named on every message already sent to them. Nothing is deleted, and
`POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/restore/` puts them back.

**This is not a "do not contact" instruction and it does not stop sends.**
A send to an archived contact still goes out. To stop messages reaching
somebody, use `POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/suppress/`,
which is checked at send time; archiving is only about your contact book.

**Safe to retry.** Archiving an archived contact answers `200` and keeps the
original `archived_at` and `archived_by`, rather than conflicting or moving
the date.

An administrator of the organization the contact belongs to, or of one
above it. Answers `200` with the contact.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer the organization this contact
  belongs to.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `409 archive_blocked` — something your product declared still holds
  this contact. `blocking` names each thing and where to close it; nothing
  was changed.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Put an archived contact back in the contact book.

Takes no body. The contact is listed by `GET /api/v1/recipients/` again,
and `archived_at` and `archived_by` are cleared. What they have agreed to
receive is untouched: a suppression recorded while they were archived
still stands.

**Safe to retry.** Restoring a contact that is not archived answers `200`
with the contact unchanged.

An administrator of the organization the contact belongs to, or of one
above it — whoever may archive a contact may restore it. Answers `200` with
the contact.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer the organization this contact
  belongs to.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `409 restore_blocked` — something your product declared stops this
  contact coming back. `blocking` names each thing and where to resolve
  it; nothing was changed.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
What one contact has agreed to, channel by channel.

One row per channel anybody has ever said anything about, carrying
`has_marketing_consent` (the yes-or-no answer, already accounting for a
later revocation), the `marketing_consented_at` and `marketing_revoked_at`
dates behind it, the quiet-hours window, and `suppressed_at`.

**A channel with no row here is not missing data.** It means nobody has said
anything about that channel, and that is a meaningful state: transactional
messages go, marketing ones do not. So an empty list is a complete answer,
not an error.

Paged with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`; the body is
`{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, and `count`
arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry the scope
  this read needs. Reading is not role-gated: anybody who can address the
  contact may see what it has agreed to. Granting and revoking consent,
  setting quiet hours and suppressing an address are the
  owner-or-administrator acts.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `messaging:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

post.description:
Record that this contact agreed to marketing on one channel.

Send `channel` (defaults to `email`). Consent is per channel: agreeing to
email says nothing about SMS.

This is what unblocks **marketing** messages. Transactional ones were never
blocked by consent. Every send checks it at the moment of sending, so this
takes effect on the next one; it does not release anything already refused.

Each call stamps `marketing_consented_at` with the time it was made, so
calling it again moves that date forward. That is how somebody who
previously withdrew consent opts back in: the later of the consent and
revocation dates is the one that counts, and neither is ever erased.

Owner or administrator of the tenant only. Answers `200` with the preference for that
channel, creating the row if this is the first thing anybody has said about
it. A contact your acting organization cannot see answers `404 not_found`.

* `400 invalid` — `channel` is not one this product knows. `errors` names
  it and nothing is recorded.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Set or clear the hours in which this contact is not to be marketed to.

Send `channel` (defaults to `email`), `start` and `end` as times of day
(`"22:00:00"`), and `timezone_name`, an IANA name such as
`"Europe/London"` (defaults to `"UTC"`). The window is read in the
**contact's** timezone, not the server's, and one that runs past midnight
(`22:00` to `07:00`) is fine.

**Send both ends or neither.** One without the other is refused with
`400 invalid` on `quiet_hours`. Sending neither is how you turn quiet hours
off. A `timezone_name` that is not a real IANA name is refused with
`400 invalid` naming that field rather than quietly falling back to UTC.

route answers `201` with `status: "suppressed"` and

post.description:
Unblock a channel for this contact. Marketing consent is not restored.

Send `channel` (defaults to `email`). Transactional messages can reach the
address again immediately.

**It does not opt anybody back in.** Suppression and marketing consent are
two separate facts and this touches only the first, so somebody who was
suppressed by a bounce and never consented to marketing ends up exactly
where they started: transactional yes, marketing no. To restore marketing,
call `POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/grant-consent/` as well —
and only if they really did agree.

**Safe to retry.** Lifting a suppression that is not there answers `200` and
changes nothing.

Owner or administrator of the tenant only. Answers `200` with the preference.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `channel` is not one this product knows.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `404 not_found` — no contact your acting organization can address has
  that id. A contact in a branch you hold no membership over answers
  this too.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `messaging:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: A key of your choosing that makes this write safe to retry. An identical retry replays the first answer and carries `Idempotent-Replayed: true`; the same key with a different body is refused rather than executed.

is only ever shown to a human — "Ada's iPhone".

**Re-registering the same token is the normal case, not an error.** A mobile
client hands its token back on every launch, after every reinstall, and
whenever the platform rotates it. So this answers `200` with the row it
already had — updated with whatever you just sent, and brought back if it
had been retired — rather than `409`. Send it as often as your client
likes.

organization you are acting as: a device belongs wherever its contact
belongs, so the branch that owns the contact is the branch that can reach
the device. There is no `organization` field on the body and there will not
be one.

**This is not consent.** Registering a device says the product *can* reach
this handset; whether it *may* is the contact's `push` preference, which is
checked inside every send. A marketing notification to somebody who has not
agreed is still refused, and
`POST /api/v1/recipients/{recipient_id}/grant-consent/` with

and no event carries it, or any part of it. Address the device by the `id`
in this answer.

get.description:
List this tenant's connections to outside systems, newest first.

Narrow with `provider` (exact), `status` (exact) or `name` (case-insensitive
substring). Sort with `ordering`, which accepts `created_at`, `updated_at`,
`name`, `provider` or `status`, each optionally prefixed with `-`; the
default is `-created_at` and any other value is refused with `400 invalid`.
Paged with `?cursor=` and `?limit=` (50 by default, 200 at most); the body
is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, and `count`
arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

post.description:
Register a link between this tenant and one outside provider.

Send `provider` (the provider's short name — letters, digits, `-` and `_`)
and `name` (yours, to tell two connections to the same provider apart).

Its inbound webhook accepts only `X-Signature-V2` unless you send
`is_signature_v2_required: false`, for a provider that cannot timestamp a request.

There are two ways to supply the credentials, and you pick one here:

* **A static API key or secret** — put it in `credentials` now, as an
  object. The connection comes back ready to use.
* **OAuth** — leave `credentials` out. The connection is created empty, and
  you then call `POST /api/v1/connections/{connection_id}/oauth/start/`,
  send the user to the URL it returns, and let the provider redirect back to
  the callback, which fills the credentials in.

Either way the credentials are stored encrypted and **no response anywhere
in this API carries one back out**. There is no field on the connection
shape that could; `has_credentials` is how you tell whether one is stored.

Answers `201` with the connection.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — a field is missing or malformed. `errors` names the
  fields and nothing is created.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `connections:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
The OAuth redirect target: exchange the provider's code for credentials.

**You do not call this yourself.** The provider's authorization page
redirects the user's browser here, carrying the `code` and `state` query
parameters, after they approve the connection. You reach this point by
calling `POST /api/v1/connections/{connection_id}/oauth/start/` and sending
the user to the `authorization_url` it gave you.

On success the credentials are stored against the connection this handshake
was started for, and the answer is `200` with that connection (without the
credentials — nothing here returns those).

**Each `state` works exactly once**, and expires ten minutes after it was
issued. Loading this URL a second time — from a browser history entry, a
proxy log, a retry — answers `400` and stores nothing. If that happens,
start a fresh handshake; there is no way to reuse a spent state.

The browser session that arrives here must belong to the same tenant that
started the handshake, or the answer is `400`.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — the `state` is unknown, has expired, has already been
  used, or belongs to another tenant. Start the handshake again.
* `403 forbidden` — storing credentials changes the connection, and you
  are not an owner or an administrator of the tenant. This is where a
  handshake a member started is refused; nothing is stored.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `404 not_found` — the connection the `state` names no longer exists.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `connections:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `connections:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

with at least one key in it; an empty object is refused with `400 invalid`.

result back, so keep your own copy of anything you cannot regenerate.

new key.

post.description:
Stop using a connection, and record why.

Send an optional `reason` — up to 500 characters, and anything longer is cut
rather than refused. It comes back on the connection as `last_error`, so
whoever finds the integration switched off later can read what happened.

This is not a delete. The connection stays, its `status` becomes `revoked`
and `revoked_at` is set, so the history of what you were connected to
survives.

**The stored credentials are destroyed, and this API cannot give them back.**
That includes the secret this connection's inbound webhook is signed with, so
deliveries the provider sends after this stop being accepted. Reconnecting
means supplying credentials again — a fresh OAuth handshake, or a new
`POST .../credentials/`.

Answers `200` with the connection.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the
  tenant.
* `404 not_found` — no connection of this tenant's has that id.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `connections:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Begin an OAuth handshake, and get the URL to send the user to.

Call this on a connection you already created (with `POST
/api/v1/connections/` and no credentials). Optionally send `redirect_uri` to
say where the provider should return the browser; omit it and this API's own
callback is used, which is the path that works out of the box.

You get back `authorization_url` — send the user's browser there — plus the
`state` that ties the return trip to this call and `expires_in`, the seconds
you have before that state stops working (600). Nothing is stored against
the connection yet: if the user closes the tab, no credentials appear and
nothing needs cleaning up. You can simply call this again.

Answers `200`. A connection id your tenant does not hold answers
`404 not_found`.

**Starting a handshake is not role-gated; finishing one is.** This call
stores nothing against the connection, so any member of the tenant may ask
for an authorization URL. The credentials land at
`GET /api/v1/connections/oauth/callback/`, which asks the same permission
`POST /api/v1/connections/{connection_id}/credentials/` asks — so a member
who starts a handshake is refused on the way back, with nothing stored.
Start one as the person who will finish it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — this connection's provider is not one this deployment
  has OAuth configured for.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `404 not_found` — no connection of this tenant's has that id.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `connections:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Where a provider POSTs its webhook deliveries for one connection.

**The provider calls this, not you**, and it takes no token and no session.
What stands in for a credential is a signature over the exact bytes of the
request body, keyed on this connection's webhook secret. There are two
schemes, and the one to send is the first:

* **`X-Signature-V2: t=<seconds>,sha256=<hex>`** — the preferred scheme.
  `t` is the moment you signed, in whole seconds since the Unix epoch, and
  the hex is an HMAC-SHA256 over the string made of `t`, a full stop, and
  the raw body bytes. The timestamp is covered by the signature, so it
  cannot be edited on the way, and a delivery whose `t` is more than
  5 minutes away from this server's clock is refused however correct the
  signature is. That window is what stops a delivery captured off the wire
  from being sent again tomorrow.
* `X-Signature: sha256=<hex>` — HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body bytes and
  nothing else. `sha256=<hex>` or the bare hex are both accepted, in either
  case. No freshness: those bytes verify as long as the secret lives, so it
  is accepted only where the connection's `is_signature_v2_required` is
  `false`, and refused with `401 timestamped_signature_required` everywhere else.

**Send one, not a hopeful pair.** When `X-Signature-V2` is present it is the
only header consulted: a correct `X-Signature` beside a stale or wrong
`X-Signature-V2` is refused. A scheme a sender can be stepped down from
would give you nothing, because anyone replaying a captured delivery would
simply drop the header that carries the window.

Send `X-Event-Type` too if you have one; it is recorded against the
delivery. Give the provider the full URL of this route, connection id and
all.

**`202` means accepted, not processed.** The body is stored and handed on to
be worked through afterwards, and this answer says only that it is safely
ours. Do not read a 202 as "the effects have happened".

Refusals you can get here:

* `401 invalid_signature` — the signature did not check out, or there is
  no connection with that id. Those answer identically and deliberately: whether the
  connection exists, whether it has a secret, what the expected signature
  was, and whether a `t` you sent was outside the 5 minutes are all
  withheld. Check that you are signing the raw body bytes with the right
  secret, that your `t` is current, and that you have not re-serialized the
  JSON on the way.
* `401 timestamped_signature_required` — a correct `X-Signature` on a connection
  that accepts only `X-Signature-V2`.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

Retry on anything other than a `202`; nothing was stored.

get.description:
List the imports your organization has staged, newest first.

**Narrow** with `status` (one of `checking`, `previewed`, `importing`,
`imported` or `failed`) and `kind`, each an exact match. **Sort** with
`ordering`: `created_at`, `updated_at` or `status`, optionally prefixed with
`-`; the default is `-created_at`.

**Pages** are `?cursor=` and `?limit=`; the body is `{"items": [...],
"has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, and `count` is `null` unless you send
`?include_count=true`.

You see the imports of the organization you are acting as — the `X-Org`
header, or your default one — and of every organization beneath it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept.
* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization, or your role does not include reading imports here.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. post.description:
Stage a CSV file you have already uploaded, as rows of one `kind`.

Answers `201` with a new import in `checking`, and `created: true`. The file
is then checked in the background: every row is validated and matched
against what you already have, and nothing is written. When `status` is
`previewed`, `counts` says how many rows would be created, updated or
refused, and `GET /api/v1/djb_imports/{id}/rows/` lists them — with the reason
for every refused row. Nothing happens to your data until you apply it.

**Staging the same file again returns the same import** — `200` and
`created: false` — for as long as that import has not failed. The file is
recognized by its contents, not its name. An `idempotency_key` you send is
honoured the same way.

The first row of the file is its header and must name the columns this kind
of import reads; the file must be UTF-8 CSV with at most 10,000 rows. A file
that is not is not refused here: the import is staged and then ends
`failed`, with `failure.code` `import_invalid` saying what was wrong.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — no importer is declared for `kind`, or the document has no
  stored version yet.
* `422 invalid_body` — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not import here, or you may not create rows of
  this `kind` — importing them needs the same permission as creating one.
* `404 not_found` — `file_id` names no document you can see.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `djb_imports:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

get.description:
One import, with where it has got to and what it found.

`status` moves `checking` → `previewed` → `importing` → `imported`, or ends
`failed`. `counts` is the preview's (`create`, `update`, `refused`) until
the import is applied, and what actually happened (`create`, `update`,
`unchanged`, `refused`) after. `apply_writes` is how many rows write: will,
then did. `failure` is the reason a failed import ended, as a refusal body.

An import belonging to an organization you cannot see answers `404
not_found`, the same answer an id that names nothing gets.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization, or your role does not include reading imports here.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `djb_imports:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `djb_imports:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

get.description:
The rows of one import's file, in file order, with what happened to each.

`outcome_preview` is what the preview said (`create`, `update` or
`refused`); `outcome` is what the apply did (`created`, `updated`,
`unchanged` or `refused`) and is empty until then. `refusal` says why a
refused row was refused — `errors` names the columns.

Narrow with `?outcome=`: `?outcome=refused` lists the refused rows before
and after the apply. Paged like every list here.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — your role does not include reading imports here.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `djb_imports:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `djb_imports:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Apply a previewed import: every row the preview accepted is written, and
every row it refused is skipped and stays listed with its reason.

Answers the import in `importing`; poll it until `imported`. Each row is
checked again as it is written — your permission to create this kind of
row, and the row's values — so a row can still end `refused` if something
changed since the preview. Pressing apply again answers the same import and
writes nothing twice.

Refusals you can get here:

* `409 conflict` — the import is still being checked, or it ended without a
  preview (it failed or was cancelled); stage the file again.
* `400 import_invalid` — the import failed because the file was refused
  whole; `errors` says what was wrong with it.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not apply imports here, or may not create rows
  of this kind.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `djb_imports:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
List the notes about one record, newest first.

**`subject` is required**: name the record as `<kind>:<id>` — for example
`?subject=widget:<id>`. Notes are only ever read through the record they
are about, so there is no list of every note.

**`show`** picks the cut: `live` (the default) lists the notes nobody has
archived, `archived` lists only the archived ones, and `all` lists both.

**Pages** are `?cursor=` and `?limit=` (50 by default, 200 at most). Send the
`next_cursor` you were given back as `?cursor=` and stop when `has_more` is
false. `count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`.

  that does not take notes. `errors` names `subject`.

  organization, or your role here does not let you read notes.
* `404 not_found` — the record is not one you can see from the organization
  you are acting as. A record in a branch alongside yours answers this too,

post.description:
Write a note about a record.

Send the `subject` — the record, as `<kind>:<id>` — and the `body`. The note
lives where the record lives: its organization is the record's, so everyone
who can see the record can read it, and nobody else can.

Answers `201` with the note.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `subject` is not `<kind>:<id>`, names a kind of record that
  does not take notes, or `body` is empty. `errors` names the field.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not write notes here, or the request resolved no
  tenant or no acting organization.
* `404 not_found` — the record is not one you can see from the organization
  you are acting as; nothing is written. A record in a branch alongside
  yours answers this, not `403`.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.

post.description:
Register a URL to receive webhooks. **The signing secret is returned once, here.**

Send:

* `url` — where we will POST each event. Required.
* `event_names` — the events you want. Leave it out or send `[]` to
  receive **every** event. Names must come from `GET /event-types/`.
* `description` — a label for your own use.

You get back `{"endpoint": {...}, "secret": "..."}`. **Save the `secret`
now.** This is the only response that will ever contain it — reading the
endpoint back later returns no secret field at all. If you lose it, call
`POST /webhook-endpoints/{id}/secret/` to get a new one; that immediately
invalidates the old one.

You cannot choose your own secret; we generate it.

**Verifying a delivery.** Each webhook arrives with two signature headers,
both keyed on your secret. Check either one. Prefer `X-Signature-V2`.

`X-Signature-V2: t=<seconds>,sha256=<hex>` — read the number after `t=`
(Unix seconds). Join it to the **exact bytes of the request body** with a
single `.` between them, so the bytes you hash begin
`1750000000.{"id":` and end with the last byte of the body. Compute
HMAC-SHA256 of that, hex-encode it, and compare it with the value after
`sha256=` using a constant-time comparison. Then check that `t` is within
**five minutes** of your own clock, and reject the delivery if it is not.
Both checks must pass. The time check is the point of this header: without
it, anyone who captured one delivery could send you the same bytes again a
year later and they would still verify. Every attempt is signed at the
moment it is sent, so a retry or a replay hours later carries a fresh `t`
and passes the time check — use `X-Event-Id`, never `t`, to spot duplicates.

`X-Signature: sha256=<hex>` — the original scheme. HMAC-SHA256 of the exact
bytes of the request body, hex-encoded and prefixed with `sha256=`. It
signs no timestamp, so a copy of a delivery verifies against it for as long
as your secret lives. It is still sent on every delivery and we will not
withdraw it without telling you first — but move to `X-Signature-V2` when
you can.

For either header: hash the bytes you received. Do not parse the JSON and
re-encode it, or the signature will not match.

Each delivery also carries `X-Event-Name`, `X-Event-Id` and
`X-Correlation-Id`; `X-Event-Id` is stable across retries and replays, so
use it to ignore duplicates.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — an `event_names` entry that is not in the catalogue, or a
  malformed URL. The `errors` object names the field. Nothing is created.
* `409 conflict` — you already have an endpoint registered on that URL.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the tenant.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `events:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
Fetch one webhook endpoint by id.

The response never contains the signing secret — there is no field for it.
Secrets are returned only when created or reissued.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no such endpoint, **or** it belongs to someone else. Those
  two cases answer identically and on purpose, so that guessing ids tells
  you nothing about what exists.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry the scope
  this read needs. Reading is not role-gated: any member of the tenant may
  see where its events go.

A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `events:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

Send only the fields you want to change; anything you leave out is kept as
it is. Send `event_names: []` to go back to receiving every event.

post.description:
Stop sending webhooks to this endpoint. Send no body.

The endpoint stays in your list with `is_active: false`, and its delivery
history is kept.

**Events that happen while it is paused are not queued up for it.** They are
simply not sent to this endpoint, and resuming later does not backfill them.
`GET /deliveries/?endpoint_id=…` shows what it did receive, ending where the
pause began.

Returns `{"items": [{"name": ..., "app": ...}], "has_more": ...,
"next_cursor": ...}`, sorted by name, walked with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`

else is rejected when you register or update the endpoint. Names read
`<area>.<thing>.<what-happened>`, for example `example.widget.created`, and
`app` tells you which part of the product emits it.

and current set. It is the same for every customer: it describes what the
product can emit, not what you happen to have subscribed to.
