get.description:
List every webhook we have tried to send you, newest first.

Returns `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`, walked
with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`; `count` arrives only with
`?include_count=true`. Failures are included — this is the log you read when a
webhook did not arrive.

Query parameters:

* `status` — `pending` (being retried), `delivered`, `failed` (the last
  attempt failed, more are coming) or `dead` (we gave up).
* `endpoint_id` — narrow to one endpoint.
* `ordering` — `created_at`, `updated_at`, `delivered_at`,
  `dead_lettered_at` or `attempts`, optionally prefixed `-`. Defaults to
  `-created_at`.

Each row is one event's delivery to one endpoint, and there is exactly one
row per pair however many times we try. So `attempts` is the running total
across every retry and every replay, `last_code` and `last_error` are what
your server said the last time we asked, `delivered_at` is when it
succeeded, and `dead_lettered_at` is when we stopped trying.

`last_code` and `last_error` are one pair about one attempt — the most
recent one — and they stay that way after we give up: dead-lettering
records that we stopped, it does not rewrite what you answered. When the
last attempt never got an answer at all (a refused connection, a timeout)
there is no status code to show, so `last_code` is `null` and `last_error`
names the transport failure.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry the scope
  this read needs. Reading is not role-gated: any member of the tenant may
  do it. It is the acts that *change* a subscription — registering,
  updating, pausing, resuming, re-keying and replaying — that need an owner
  or an administrator.
* `403 forbidden` — your role here does not let you read deliveries. A
  role with no read of this kind reads none of them: ask an administrator
  for the permission, or act under an organization where you hold it.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `events:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `events:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Send a given-up webhook again. Send no body.

**This re-sends the event to every active endpoint subscribed to it, not
just this one** — including endpoints that received it successfully the
first time. They will see the same `X-Event-Id` again, so your receivers
should ignore an event id they have already processed.

The response is the delivery row as it stands the moment the replay is
queued; the attempt itself happens shortly afterwards. Poll
`GET /deliveries/` and watch `attempts` and `status` to see how it went.
The row keeps its original `dead_lettered_at`, so the record that it once
failed is not erased by a successful replay.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — this delivery was never given up on. One that is still
  `pending` or `failed` is still being retried automatically, and replaying
  it would just send a duplicate.
* `404 not_found` — no such delivery, or it is not yours.
* `403 forbidden` — you are not an owner or an administrator of the tenant.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `events:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

409.description:
**`conflict`** — Something that already exists holds the name, the identifier or the state this write asked for. Nothing was written.
- Re-read the row and retry against what is true now (`self:reread`)
- Ask for the first answer back instead of a second attempt (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`idempotency_key_reuse`** — This Idempotency-Key has already been used, for a different request. The fingerprint covers the method, the path and the body, so one changed byte is a different request under a key that is already spoken for. Nothing was written.
- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`merge_blocked`** — These two cannot be merged while something still holds them apart. Nothing was written, and neither record changed.
- See what holds them apart (`self:reread`)

**`merged`** — This was merged into another record and can no longer be changed. Nothing was written; the answer names the record it became.
- Open the record it became (`route:widget-detail`)

**`archived`** — This is archived. It can be read, and it cannot be changed until it is restored. Nothing was written.
- Restore it first (`route:widget-restore`)

**`stale_version`** — Somebody else changed this since you read it, so your change was not saved. Nothing was written; the answer says which version it has now.
- Read it again, then make your change to what is there now (`self:reread`)

409.description:
**`conflict`** — Something that already exists holds the name, the identifier or the state this write asked for. Nothing was written.
- Re-read the row and retry against what is true now (`self:reread`)
- Ask for the first answer back instead of a second attempt (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`idempotency_key_reuse`** — This Idempotency-Key has already been used, for a different request. The fingerprint covers the method, the path and the body, so one changed byte is a different request under a key that is already spoken for. Nothing was written.
- Resend the identical body to replay the first answer (`header:Idempotency-Key`)
- Give a genuinely different write a key of its own (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`in_progress`** — The first request under this Idempotency-Key is still running, so its answer does not exist yet. Yours was not run — which is the point: two concurrent retries of one write must not both write.
- Wait, then retry the identical request (`header:Idempotency-Key`)

**`archived`** — This is archived. It can be read, and it cannot be changed until it is restored. Nothing was written.
- Restore it first (`route:portal_request-restore`)

post.description:
Ask about a widget, in your own words.

Send the `widget_id` of a widget you can see, a `note` and, optionally, a
`priority` (`low`, `normal` or `high`). It lives where you are acting — no
field sets it — so you read it back, and so do the people above you.

Answers `201` with the request.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `note` is empty or too long; `errors` names it.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not send requests here.
* `404 not_found` — the widget is not one you can see from where you are
  acting; nothing is sent. A widget in a branch alongside yours answers
  this, exactly as one that does not exist.
* `409 archived` — the widget is archived; nothing is sent.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `422 invalid_body` — `priority` is not one of the three; nothing is sent.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `portal_requests:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

- Check the role your membership gives you here (`self:membership`)
- Ask somebody who administers this organization (`header:X-Org`)

**`insufficient_scope`** — This token is limited to a set of scopes, and this operation needs one it does not carry. Nothing was read and nothing was written. The limit is on the token, not on the person who minted it — the same person signed in with a browser, or holding a wider token, may well be allowed to do this.
- Mint a new token that carries the scope named here — the operation that mints one is under API tokens (`docs:openapi`)
- See which scope each operation needs, beside the operation (`docs:openapi`)

**`addressing_header_not_honoured`** — You are who you say you are, and this request named a place it cannot act in. An address you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one your acting organization does not cover, and an empty value are all answered exactly the same way — the refusal is about what you asked for, never about what exists, so it confirms nothing. Nothing was read and nothing was written. Leaving the header out is different and still works: it acts in your default membership.
- Name a tenant you hold a membership in, or send no such header (`header:X-Tenant`)
- Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)
- Check which memberships you actually hold (`self:membership`)

**`no_acting_scope`** — You are who you say you are, and this request resolved no workspace, or no part of one, for you to act in — you hold no membership it could act under. Nothing was read and nothing was written.
- Check which memberships you actually hold (`self:membership`)
- Name a tenant you hold a membership in (`header:X-Tenant`)
- Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)

get.description:
List the archives your organization has asked for, newest first.

**Narrow** with `status`, which is one of `pending`, `running`, `completed`
or `failed`. It is an exact match, so `?status=fail` finds nothing and
`?status=failed` finds the failures.

**Sort** with `ordering`. It accepts `created_at`, `completed_at` or
`status`, each optionally prefixed with `-` for descending, and the default
is `-created_at`. Any other value is refused with `400 invalid` rather than
quietly ignored.

**Pages** are `?cursor=` and `?limit=` (50 by default, 200 at most). The
body is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`: send the
`next_cursor` you were given back as `?cursor=` for the following page, and
stop when `has_more` is false. A cursor is opaque — never build or edit one.

**`count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`**, because a total
costs a second pass over the matches.

**What you can see** depends on the organization you are acting as — the
`X-Org` header, or your default organization if you send none. You get that
organization's exports and those of every organization beneath it. Exports
belonging to an organization alongside yours, or above it, are not in the
list.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — your role does not include reading exports here.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `exports:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `exports:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Ask for an archive of your data. Answers `201` straight away with an export
in `pending`; the archive itself is built in the background.

`scope` decides how much goes in it:

* `organization` (the default) — everything the organization you are acting
  as can see, and everything beneath it. This needs no special permission,
  because it is the same data you can already page through one request at a
  time.
* `tenant` — the whole account, including the tables that belong to the
  account as a whole rather than to any one organization. This needs
  administrator rights at the top of the account, and answers `403
  forbidden` otherwise.

Send `idempotency_key` with your own name for the request — `nightly-2026-08-24`,
a ticket number, anything stable. Asking again with the same one returns the
export you already have instead of building a second copy of your data.

Poll `GET /api/v1/exports/{id}/` until `status` is `completed`, then use
`download_url` if it is set and `download_path` otherwise. The `manifest` on
the export says exactly which tables are in the archive, how many rows each
has, and which columns and tables were left out and why — read it before you
download, not after.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `scope` is not one of `organization` or `tenant`, or the
  body carried a field this endpoint does not accept. `errors` names the
  fields and nothing is created.
* `403 forbidden` — you asked for the whole account and you are not an
  owner or an administrator of it, or the request resolved no acting
  organization.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` header for a different request, or the first request
  under it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

get.description:
One export, with where it has got to and how to fetch it.

While `status` is `pending` or `running` there is nothing to download yet
and both download fields are `null`. When it is `completed`, use
`download_url` if it is set — that is a temporary link straight to storage —
and `download_path` otherwise, which is a path on this API that you fetch
with your usual credential. Reading `download_url or download_path` is
correct on either kind of deployment.

When it is `failed`, `error` says what went wrong and nothing was written:
there is no partial archive to fetch. Ask for a new export.

`expires_at` is when the archive and this record are deleted. It is about a
month after you asked, and it is not extendable — download what you need
before then.

An export belonging to an organization you cannot see answers
`404 not_found`, the same answer an id that names nothing gets.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — your role does not include reading exports here.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `exports:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `exports:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

**`insufficient_scope`** — This token is limited to a set of scopes, and this operation needs one it does not carry. Nothing was read and nothing was written. The limit is on the token, not on the person who minted it — the same person signed in with a browser, or holding a wider token, may well be allowed to do this.

- Name a tenant you hold a membership in (`header:X-Tenant`)
- Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)

get.description:
Fetch the archive itself: a zip file, streamed.

Inside it there is one `models/<app>.<Model>.jsonl` file per table — one JSON
object per line, in the table's own column names — and a `manifest.json`
listing every table in the archive with its row count, the columns that were
left out and why, the tables a single-organization export could not carry,
and the tables left out because whoever asked for the archive may not read
them (`omitted_models`, each with the reason `unreadable`). The manifest is
the same document the export record shows you, so you can check what you are
about to download before you download it.

**This route redirects.** It answers `302` with a short-lived signed link to
the archive in object storage, and your client follows it to the bytes — the
same link the export record publishes as `download_url`. Any client that
follows redirects needs no change (`curl -L`, a browser, `requests`); a
client that does not should read `download_url` off the record instead.

Send your usual credential to THIS route: the redirect is issued only to a
caller who may read the export. The link it hands back carries its own
signature, is good for a few minutes, and needs no credential of yours — so
treat it as the secret it is and do not paste it anywhere durable.

An export that has not finished, one that failed, and one whose archive has
already expired all answer `404 not_found`. So does an export belonging to
an organization you cannot see.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — your role does not include reading exports here.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see, or there is no
  archive on it to fetch.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `exports:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `exports:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

400.description:
**`invalid`** — The input does not hold. The answer names each field that is wrong and why, in the schema's own field names, so the failure can be pointed at rather than guessed at.
- Read the failing fields and resend (`field:errors`)
- Read the shape this endpoint accepts (`docs:openapi`)

**`invalid_cursor`** — That cursor is not one this API issued for this walk. A cursor is opaque and signed, and it names a position in ONE list in ONE ordering — editing one, presenting one to a different list, or replaying one against a different sort order has no meaning to answer. Nothing was skipped and nothing was lost.
- Start the walk again with no cursor (`field:cursor`)
- Follow the next_cursor the last response gave you (`field:next_cursor`)

get.description:
The documents your organization has stored, newest first.

**Archived documents are not here by default.** Archiving takes a document out
of everyone's working set, and this is the working set. `?show=archived` lists
the archived documents and only them; `?show=all` lists both; `?show=live` is
the default. A document you archived is still readable by its id, and its
versions are still fetchable. There is no `?archived=` — it is refused, naming
`show`, rather than ignored.

**Filed against a record:** `?subject=<kind>:<id>` — for example
`?subject=widget:<id>` — lists the documents filed against that record. A
record you cannot see answers `404 not_found`, exactly as one that does not
exist does, and a kind that does not take documents answers `400 invalid`
naming `subject`.

**Narrow** with `purpose`, which matches exactly — whatever short label you
filed the document under — and with `filename`, which matches anywhere in the
name, so `?filename=invoice` finds `invoice-2026-08.pdf`.

**Sort** with `ordering`. It accepts `created_at`, `updated_at` or `filename`,
each optionally prefixed with `-` for descending, and the default is
`-created_at`. Any other value is refused with `400 invalid` rather than
quietly ignored.

**Pages** are `?cursor=` and `?limit=` (50 by default, 200 at most). The body
is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`: send the
`next_cursor` you were given back as `?cursor=` for the following page, and
stop when `has_more` is false. A cursor is opaque — never build or edit one.

**`count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`**, because a total
costs a second pass over the matches.

**What you can see** depends on the organization you are acting as — the
`X-Org` header, or your default organization if you send none. You get that
organization's documents and those of every organization beneath it. Documents
belonging to an organization alongside yours, or above it, are not in the list.

Each document says which version is `current_version`; `0` means nothing has
finished uploading yet, which is a real state and not a placeholder.

**Each document carries `allowed_acts`** — what you may do to it as it stands:
an administrator reads `archive` on a live document and `restore` on an
archived one, a member reads neither. The page carries its own `allowed_acts`
too, holding `create` when you may file a document where you are acting.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, a
  filter value was malformed, `?show=` was not `live`, `archived` or `all`
  (or `?archived=` was sent), or `?subject=` was not `<kind>:<id>` or names a
  kind that takes no documents. The response names the parameter.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token authenticated and its ceiling does not
  carry `files:read`. Mint one that does.
* `404 not_found` — `?subject=` names a record you cannot see, or none at all.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `files:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Start a new document. Answers `201` with the document, its first version, and
**where to PUT the bytes** — the bytes never travel through this API.

Three steps, and the second one does not touch us at all:

1. `POST` here. You get back `upload_url`, good for `expires_in` seconds.
2. `PUT` your bytes to that URL with **two headers**: `Content-Type` set to
   exactly the `content_type` you sent here, and `If-None-Match: *`. Both are
   part of the signature, so leaving either out is refused by storage rather
   than accepted leniently — and the second is what stops the same link being
   replayed later over bytes that have already been finalized.
3. `POST /files/{id}/versions/{n}/confirm` to tell us you have finished. We
   then fetch the object ourselves, measure it, and record what we measured.

Nothing is stored until step 3 completes: until then `current_version` is `0`
and the version's `status` is `pending`.

`size_bytes` is what you expect to upload. We check it against the limit and
never record it — what gets recorded is what we measure when we read the
object back, so a declared size that turns out to be wrong changes nothing
except that the true size is what you are metered for.

`purpose` is your own short label — `contract`, `lab-result`, `invoice`. It is
an open vocabulary on purpose: what you file is your word for it.

**Where it lands** is the organization you are acting as — the `X-Org` header,
or your default organization — and there is no field here to send instead. A
request that resolves no organization is refused rather than filed at the top
of your account.

**Filing against a record:** send `subject` as `<kind>:<id>` — for example
`widget:<id>` — and the document is filed against that record and lands in
**the record's organization**, so everyone who can read the record can read
it; list them with `GET /files/?subject=<kind>:<id>`. A record you cannot see
answers `404 not_found`, the same as one that does not exist, and a kind that
does not take documents answers `400 invalid` naming `subject`.

**Your credential must belong to a person.** A document records who filed it,
for as long as it exists, so a machine token with no user behind it is refused
with `400 invalid` naming `uploaded_by`.

Send `Idempotency-Key` with your own opaque value and a retry of the identical
request replays the first answer — the same document, the same version, and the
same upload URL — instead of filing a second document.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — the declared size is above the limit, your credential
  resolved no person, the request resolved no acting organization, or
  `subject` was malformed or names a kind that takes no documents. Nothing
  was created.
* `422 invalid_body` — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept,
  or one was missing or the wrong type. `errors` names the fields.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not file documents in this organization.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:write`.
* `404 not_found` — `subject` names a record you cannot see, or none at all.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` header for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

`current_version` is `0` while nothing has finished uploading. `archived_at` and
`archived_by` are `null` while the document is in the working set, and say when
and by whom once somebody has archived it — an archived document is still

link, and every change to it refused with `409 archived` until it is restored.

`allowed_acts` says what you may do to it as it stands — `archive` for an
administrator of its organization while it is live, `restore` once archived,
neither for a member.

A document belonging to an organization you cannot see answers `404 not_found`,

post.description:
Take a document out of everyone's working set. It disappears from the list, and
nothing new can be added to it.

**This is not a delete, and the difference matters.** Every version stays
readable, every version stays fetchable on a signed link, and the stored bytes
remain exactly where they were. What changes is that the document stops
appearing in the list (find it with `?show=archived`) and that every change to
it — `POST /files/{id}/versions` included — is refused with `409 archived` until
it is restored with `POST /files/{id}/restore/`.

**It takes administrator rights**, unlike filing and replacing, which are open
to anybody in the account: you must administer the part of the organization the
document belongs to. Archiving makes your own record less complete without
making anything smaller, so it is kept to the people who administer that part of
the organization.

The answer carries `archived_at` and `archived_by` — when, and who. Archiving
something already archived answers `200` with the document unchanged — the
first archive's date and archiver kept — and does nothing: safe to retry.

**Takes no body.** A client that still sends `{}` is answered exactly the
same; nothing reads it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer the part of the organization this
  document belongs to.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:write`.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `409 archive_blocked` — something still depends on this document; the answer
  names what. Nothing was changed.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

post.description:
Put an archived document back in everyone's working set. It is listed again,
and it takes new versions again.

Nothing about its versions or its stored bytes changes — archiving never moved
them, so there is nothing to put back but the document's place in the list.
`archived_at` and `archived_by` read `null` again.

**It takes the same administrator rights archiving does**: you must administer
the part of the organization the document belongs to.

Restoring a document that is not archived answers `200` with it unchanged and
does nothing — safe to retry.

**Takes no body.** A client that still sends `{}` is answered exactly the
same; nothing reads it.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 forbidden` — you do not administer the part of the organization this
  document belongs to.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:write`.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `409 restore_blocked` — something stops this document coming back; the answer
  names what. Nothing was changed.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Ask for a short-lived private link to one version of a document, and fetch the
bytes from it directly.

Send an empty body — `{}` — for the current version, or `{"version": 2}` to pin
the link to a particular one. **A link issued for version 2 keeps serving
version 2's bytes** after version 3 lands and becomes current: every version
has its own object, and what an already-issued link means never changes.

The link needs no credential of yours and works for anyone holding it until it
expires, in `expires_in` seconds. **Treat it as the secret it is**: do not
email it, do not put it in a URL bar somebody screenshots, do not store it.
When it expires, storage refuses it in its own words — a `403` that is not from
this API and does not look like one — and the remedy is to ask here again.
There is no longer-lived link.

The answer also carries `sha256` and `size_bytes`, which are **what we measured
by reading the object ourselves**, never what the uploader declared. Check the
bytes you fetched against them.

**Every issuance is recorded** against the version it was issued for, together
with who asked and which organization they were acting as. What we cannot
record is whether the link was used: the fetch goes to storage, not to us. So
the trail says a link existed, and asking again for the bytes creates a new
entry.

A document belonging to an organization you cannot see answers `404 not_found`
— and so does a version that does not exist, a version whose bytes have not
finished uploading, and a document that has never had one finish. All four are
the same answer on purpose: a link request must never be a way of finding out
whether somebody's document is there.

Refusals you can get here:

* `422 invalid_body` — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept,
  or `version` was not a positive whole number.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not read this organization's documents.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:write`.
  Issuing a link records an entry against the document, which is what puts this
  operation on the writing side of a token's ceiling.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see, or there are no
  stored bytes at the version you asked for.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
Every version this document has had, newest first — what each one was called
when it arrived, how big it is, its digest, and whether its bytes have landed.

`size_bytes` and `sha256` are **what we measured** by reading the object, not
what the uploader told us. They are `null` and empty while a version is still
`pending`, which is the honest answer rather than a zero that reads like a
measurement.

Versions are never rewritten. Replacing a document adds a version beside the
old one, so a digest you recorded stays true about the bytes it was taken from
forever.

**Sort** with `ordering`: `version` or `created_at`, optionally prefixed with
`-`, default `-version`.

**Pages** are `?cursor=` and `?limit=`, and `count` is `null` unless you send
`?include_count=true`, exactly as on the document list.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:read`.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see, or a `?cursor=` you
  sent belongs to a different walk.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `files:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

post.description:
Add a new version beside the current one, and get somewhere to PUT its bytes.

**The old version is untouched.** It stays readable, stays fetchable on a
signed link, and stays true for anything that already quoted its digest. What
changes is which version a reader who names none gets — and that only changes
once the new one has finished uploading and we have measured it.

The three steps are the same as filing a document: `POST` here for an
`upload_url`, `PUT` the bytes to it with `Content-Type` and `If-None-Match: *`,
then `POST .../confirm`. Until the confirm completes, `current_version` still
points at the old version and the new one's `status` is `pending`.

There is no `filename` here on purpose: replacing a document does not rename
it. A document that needs a different name is a different document.

An **archived** document cannot be replaced — that is what archiving is for —
and answers `409 archived`; restore it first.

Send `Idempotency-Key` and a retry of the identical request replays the first
answer instead of allocating a second version.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — the declared size is above the limit, your credential
  resolved no person, or the request resolved no acting organization.
* `422 invalid_body` — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not add versions in this organization.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:write`.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see.
* `409 archived` — the document is archived, so nothing new goes into it.
  Restore it with `POST /files/{id}/restore/` first.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` header for a different request, or the first request under
  it has not finished.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

post.description:
Tell us the bytes are up. Answers `202` immediately and starts the check in the
background.

**We take nothing on trust here.** Confirming does not mark anything stored: it
starts a job that fetches the object from storage, streams it, and measures its
size and its SHA-256 itself. Only then does the version become `stored`, get
its digest, and — if it is the highest one stored — become the document's
`current_version`. A confirm for an upload that never happened produces a job
that finds nothing, not a version that claims to be there.

So the version in this response is still `pending`. Poll
`GET /files/{id}/versions/` until it says `stored`.

`idempotency_key` is **your own name for this upload** and is required. It is
not what stops a double confirm — confirming twice joins the check already
running, because the job's identity comes from the version itself — it is what
ties this call to whatever you were doing in your own system, in the record we
keep of it.

Confirming a version whose bytes we have already measured answers `202` and
starts nothing. The question has already been answered, by evidence.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `idempotency_key` was blank, or the request resolved no
  acting organization.
* `422 invalid_body` — the body carried a field this endpoint does not accept.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant or no acting
  organization. Send `X-Tenant` and `X-Org` naming ones you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — you may not add versions in this organization.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token's ceiling does not carry `files:write`.
* `404 not_found` — nothing has that id where you can see, or that document has
  no version with that number.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `files:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

get.description:
List every kind of thing this product can find, so you can narrow a search
to one of them.

Returns `{"items": [{"kind": ..., "app": ...}], "has_more": ...,
"next_cursor": ...}`, in alphabetical order, walked with `?cursor=` and
`?limit=`. `count` arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

Every value `kinds` accepts on the search endpoint is here, and nothing
else is: a name that is not on this list is refused there rather than
quietly searched for and not found. `app` says which part of the product
owns those records — that is where you fetch one in full once a search has
pointed at it.

This list is generated from the running product, so it is always complete
and current. It is the same for every customer: it describes what this
product can search, not what you happen to have. A deployment that has made
nothing searchable answers with an empty list, which is a true and useful
answer — it is what tells you that no search here will ever find anything.

**It does not shrink to what YOU may read**, and that is deliberate: a kind
you may not read is still a kind this product has, and this list is the
product's vocabulary rather than your entitlement. The search endpoint is
where your entitlement applies — it searches the kinds you may read and
refuses a kind you name and may not.

  naming one you belong to.

* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. get.description:
Find things by typing words. One search covers every kind of record this
product has made searchable, and answers with the best matches first.

**`q`** is what you are looking for — words, part of a name, a reference
number. An empty `q` matches everything you can see, which is a useful way
to page through a kind.

**Narrow** with `kinds`, a comma-separated list of the kinds
`GET /search/kinds/` lists. Leave it out to search everything. A name that
is not on that list is **refused** — `400 invalid`, naming what you sent and
what this product does declare — so a typo and an empty product are never
the same answer.

**Pages** are `?cursor=` and `?limit=` (20 by default, 200 at most). The body
is `{"items": [...], "has_more": ..., "next_cursor": ...}`: send the
`next_cursor` you were given back as `?cursor=` for the following page, and
stop when `has_more` is false. A cursor is opaque and belongs to the search
that produced it — never build one, and never send a cursor from a different
endpoint.

**`count` is `null` unless you send `?include_count=true`**. When you do ask,
it is exact, and it counts only what you can see — including when the answer
is `0`. `null` means "nobody counted"; it never stands in for zero.

**What you can see** depends on the organization you are acting as — the
`X-Org` header, or your default organization if you send none. You get that
organization's records and those of every organization beneath it, and
nothing else: a word that appears only in a record you cannot reach produces
no hit and adds nothing to the count.

**Results can lag a change by seconds.** A record you just created appears
once the change has made its way to the index. If you need a list that is
true the instant you write it, use that record's own list endpoint — this is
a search, and it trades a second of freshness for finding things by their
words.

**`engine`** in the response says which engine answered: `meili` normally,
`postgres` while the index is unreachable, when matching is plainer and
typos are not forgiven. What you can see does not change either way.

**One field here is deliberately not a report of what happened, and it is
this one.** When the answer is empty because you can see nothing — you act
as no organization in this account — no engine is asked at all, and the page
still names the engine this deployment searches with. That is on purpose: a page you are not
entitled to and a page that genuinely matched nothing are the same page,
down to the byte, so that nobody can use this endpoint to find out whether a
record they cannot reach exists. Everything else in the body is exactly what
it says.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no account. Send `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `403 forbidden` — `kinds` named a kind your role does not include reading.
  Leave `kinds` out to search everything you can read; a kind you may not
  read is simply not in the results.
* `400 invalid` — `kinds` named something this product cannot search. The
  message says what you sent and lists what it does have;
  `GET /search/kinds/` is the same list. **`403` and `400` are different
  answers on purpose**: `400` means no such kind anywhere, `403` means that
  kind exists and is not yours.
* `400 invalid_cursor` — the cursor was edited, or came from a different
  endpoint. Start the walk again without one.
* `404 not_found` — the cursor was minted for a different account.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.
* `503 search_unavailable` — **not** the index being down; that is answered
  from Postgres above. This means no engine could answer at all. Retry;
  nothing is wrong with your request.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `search:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `search:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

allOf.description:
The windows a total is asked for over. Two, and adding a third is a diff.

A `StrEnum` because these values are written by hand into a tenant's settings
JSON and read back out of it: `"month"` in the config file and
`PeriodKind.MONTH` in the code have to be the same object without anybody
mapping between them.

**No `year`, no `week`, no arbitrary range** — not because they are hard, but
because every one of them is a bucketing decision a rollup will one day have
to materialise, and the set that gets materialised should be the set somebody
chose. A caller wanting an arbitrary window builds a `Period` directly.

get.description:
What your organization has consumed in one window, meter by meter, with the
daily subtotals each total was added up from.

**A meter counts things used** — tokens, bytes, messages — under a name like
`files.storage.bytes`. Every quantity here is a **quantity and never a
price**: what any of it costs is not something this endpoint knows or says.
Which meters exist is not something to guess at: `GET /meters/` lists every
one this deployment declares, and a name that is not on that list is refused
here rather than answered with zero.

**Choose the window** with `period`, which is `month` (the default) or
`day`, and `on`, which is any date inside the window you want — send
`?period=month&on=2026-08-12` for the whole of that August. Leave `on` out
and you get the window containing today. Windows are counted in **UTC**, so
a report never changes because somebody moved.

**Narrow to particular meters** by repeating `meters`:
`?meters=files.storage.bytes`. A meter you name
that recorded nothing comes back at zero rather than being left out, so you
can tell "none" from "I asked the wrong question" — and a meter this
deployment does not declare is **refused** (`400 invalid`, naming what is
declared) rather than zero-filled, which is the other half of being able to
tell those apart. Name none and you get whatever the window actually holds.

**Every number is a JSON string**, not a JSON number — `"1240.0000"`, not
`1240` — so that no client's float handling can change a figure on the way
in. Parse them as decimals.

Each meter's total is a **measured** number: `value` is the window's total,
`basis.formula` is the string `sum(day_totals)`, and `basis.inputs` maps
every date in the window to that day's subtotal — including the days that
contributed nothing, so you can check the arithmetic without asking a second
question. Add the inputs up and you get the value.

**What you can see** depends on the organization you are acting as — the
`X-Org` header, or your default organization if you send none. You get that
organization's consumption and that of every organization beneath it. A
branch alongside yours, or above it, is not in the total. **An `X-Org` you
send that we cannot resolve is refused** (`403 addressing_header_not_honoured`)
rather than quietly ignored: a mistyped hat must never come back as a bill of
zero.

**There is no way to write usage here, and that is deliberate.** Consumption
is recorded by the platform as it happens, so nothing you send could add to
it or take away from it — a figure you believe is wrong is a conversation
with us, and the correction is a new entry that says what it corrects and
why, leaving both readable.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `period` was something other than `day` or `month`, `on`
  was not a date, or a `meters` entry is not a meter this deployment
  declares. The response says which parameter, and for a meter it says what
  the vocabulary is and where to list it.
* `403 no_acting_scope` — the request resolved no tenant. Send an `X-Tenant`
  naming one you belong to.
* `403 addressing_header_not_honoured` — the `X-Tenant` or `X-Org` you sent
  is not one you can act as. Name one you belong to, or send neither and act
  as your defaults.
* `403 forbidden` — this credential may not read usage.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token authenticated and its ceiling does
  not carry `usage:read`. Mint one that does.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `usage:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `usage:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

get.description:
List every meter this deployment counts things under.

Returns `{"items": [{"name": ..., "app": ...}], "has_more": ...,
"next_cursor": ...}`, sorted by name, walked with `?cursor=` and `?limit=`
(50 at a time by default, 200 at most). `count` arrives only with
`?include_count=true`.

**A meter counts things used** — tokens, bytes, messages — under a name that
reads `<area>.<thing>.<unit>`, for example `files.storage.bytes`, and `app`
tells you which part of the product spends it. Every value you can put in
`GET /usage/?meters=` is here; anything else is refused there rather than
answered with a zero, so this list is how you tell a meter that recorded
nothing from a name we do not have.

This list is generated from the running system, so it is always the complete
and current set. It is the same for every customer: it describes what the
product can meter, not what you happen to have consumed. **A quantity is
never a price** — what any of this costs is not something these endpoints
know or say.

Refusals you can get here:

* `403 insufficient_scope` — the token you sent does not carry the scope
  this read needs. Reading is not role-gated: this is the product's own
  vocabulary, the same for every customer, and any member may read it.
* `400 invalid_cursor` — the `?cursor=` was edited, or came from a different
  endpoint. Start the walk again without one.
* `404 not_found` — the cursor was minted for a different account.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `usage:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `usage:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

get.description:
List the background jobs started in the tenant you are acting in, newest
first.

A background job is any piece of work the API does not finish while you
wait — sending a message, syncing an integration, onboarding a record. Each
one gets a row here the moment it is started, and the row is updated as the
job progresses.

By default you get **only the jobs you started yourself**. Send
`mine=false` to see everything anybody in this tenant started, including your
colleagues' jobs. A few jobs have no recorded starter — jobs begun before
this endpoint existed, and jobs the platform runs for itself — and those
appear only when `mine=false`.

Filter with `status` (`running`, `completed` or `failed`) and `type` (the
job's name, for example `WidgetOnboardingWorkflow`). Sort with `ordering`,
which accepts `started_at`, `finished_at`, `created_at`, `updated_at`,
`status` or `type`, each optionally prefixed with `-` to reverse it;
anything else is rejected with `invalid`. Walk it with `?cursor=` and
`?limit=`; `count` arrives only with `?include_count=true`.

Each row tells you `status`, when it `started_at` and `finished_at`, who
started it (`started_by_email`), and — when it failed — `error`, which is
the underlying failure, not a generic wrapper. `run_id` is the identifier
the job has in the execution engine; it is briefly empty for a job that has
just been started and not yet handed over.

Refusals you can get here:

* `400 invalid` — `?ordering=` named a field this list does not accept, or
  a filter value was malformed. The response says what you may sort by.
* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant. Send `X-Tenant` naming
  one you belong to.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `runs:read` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted. A token carrying `runs:write` satisfies this too: within one section, the write scope includes the read.

Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

post.description:
Run a failed background job again, from the beginning.

Send no body. The job is restarted with **the same input it was originally
given** — the execution engine still has it, so you do not need to know
what it was or to repeat the original request. The job keeps the same `id`
and the same `workflow_id`.

You get the job back with `status` set to `running`, `error` cleared and
`finished_at` empty. `run_id` is briefly empty and fills in once the engine
has accepted the restart; poll this job's `GET` endpoint to follow it.

**Restarting re-does everything the job had already done** before it
failed, including anything it sent or wrote. Jobs in this API are built to
be safe to run twice, but be aware that a restart is a genuine re-run and
not a resume from the point of failure.

You may only restart **jobs you started yourself**.

Refusals you can get here:

* `404 not_found` — no such job, a job belonging to another tenant, a job
  one of your colleagues started, or a job with no recorded starter. All
  four give the same answer on purpose, so this endpoint cannot be used to
  discover whether an id is real. If a colleague's job needs restarting,
  ask them to do it.
* `409 conflict`, *still running* — the job has not failed; there is
  nothing to restart. Wait for it to finish, and restart it only if it
  fails.
* `409 conflict`, *already finished* — the job succeeded. Running the same
  work again is a new job, not a repeat of that one, so start it through
  whichever endpoint started it the first time.
* `409 conflict`, *too old* — the job started more than 30 days ago and the
  record of what it was asked to do is no longer kept, so there is nothing
  to restart from. Start the work again from the endpoint that originally
  started it.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `runs:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

parameters.name: X-Tenant
parameters.description: Which tenant to act in, by slug. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's tenant, which is the ordinary case. **Send it** and it is honoured or the request is refused: a tenant you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one a pinned token may not act in, and an empty value are all refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) — identically, so the refusal says nothing about what exists. Nothing is read and nothing is written. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: X-Org
parameters.description: Which PART of the tenant to act as, by slug — the hat you are wearing. It must be an organization you hold a membership on, or above; roles inherit downwards only, so naming your parent or a sibling is not wearable. **Omit it** and you act in your default membership's own node. **Send one you cannot wear** — or an empty value — and the request is refused with `addressing_header_not_honoured` (403) rather than answered under another hat. The value is trimmed and lower-cased before it is matched, and an empty or whitespace-only value counts as SENT.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: A key of your choosing that makes this write safe to retry. An identical retry replays the first answer and carries `Idempotent-Replayed: true`; the same key with a different body is refused rather than executed.

Idempotent-Replayed.description: `true` when this answer is a replay of an earlier identical request.

403.description:
**`forbidden`** — You are who you say you are, and this is still not yours to do here. The row exists and you can see it; the action is what was refused.
- Check the role your membership gives you here (`self:membership`)
- Ask somebody who administers this organization (`header:X-Org`)

**`insufficient_scope`** — This token is limited to a set of scopes, and this operation needs one it does not carry. Nothing was read and nothing was written. The limit is on the token, not on the person who minted it — the same person signed in with a browser, or holding a wider token, may well be allowed to do this.
- Mint a new token that carries the scope named here — the operation that mints one is under API tokens (`docs:openapi`)
- See which scope each operation needs, beside the operation (`docs:openapi`)

**`addressing_header_not_honoured`** — You are who you say you are, and this request named a place it cannot act in. An address you hold no membership in, one that does not exist, one your acting organization does not cover, and an empty value are all answered exactly the same way — the refusal is about what you asked for, never about what exists, so it confirms nothing. Nothing was read and nothing was written. Leaving the header out is different and still works: it acts in your default membership.
- Name a tenant you hold a membership in, or send no such header (`header:X-Tenant`)
- Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)
- Check which memberships you actually hold (`self:membership`)

**`no_acting_scope`** — You are who you say you are, and this request resolved no workspace, or no part of one, for you to act in — you hold no membership it could act under. Nothing was read and nothing was written.
- Check which memberships you actually hold (`self:membership`)
- Name a tenant you hold a membership in (`header:X-Tenant`)
- Name an organization you hold a role on, or above — roles inherit downwards only (`header:X-Org`)

post.description:
Ask a background job that is still running to stop.

Send no body. **This is a request, not an instant result.** The job is told
to stop; it then gets to finish tidying up whatever it was part-way through,
and only when it has actually stopped does its record say so. Some jobs stop
within a second and a few take longer.

So the job comes back from this call **exactly as it was** — `status` is
still `running` — and that is not a mistake. Poll this job's `GET` endpoint:
its `status` becomes `cancelled` once the job has really stopped, and
`finished_at` fills in at the same moment. A job that had already finished
the last of its work before your request reached it may still end
`completed`; nothing is rolled back by stopping a job, so anything it had
already sent or written stays sent and written.

A stopped job is **not** a failed one. `cancelled` and `failed` are separate
words on purpose, and a job you stopped cannot be restarted with the restart
endpoint — start the work again where it was started the first time.

You may only stop **jobs you started yourself**.

Refusals you can get here:

* `401 unauthenticated` — no usable credential resolved: none was sent, or
  the bearer token was wrong, expired or revoked. Sign in, or send
  `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
* `403 insufficient_scope` — the bearer token authenticated but is not
  scoped for this. Mint one that carries the scope named in the response.
* `403 forbidden` — the request resolved no tenant, or you do not have
  standing to stop background jobs here. Send `X-Tenant` naming a tenant you
  belong to.
* `404 not_found` — no such job, a job belonging to another tenant, a job
  one of your colleagues started, or a job with no recorded starter. All
  four give the same answer on purpose, so this endpoint cannot be used to
  discover whether an id is real. If a colleague's job needs stopping, ask
  them to stop it.
* `409 conflict` — the job has already finished, one way or another, so
  there is nothing left to stop. The message names the state it is in.
* `409 idempotency_key_reuse` / `409 in_progress` — you reused an
  `Idempotency-Key` for a different request, or the first request under it
  has not finished. Resend the identical request, or use a new key.
* `429 rate_limited` — wait for the `Retry-After` seconds and try again.

**Token scope:** a bearer token must carry `runs:write` to make this call. A token minted with no limit carries every scope, and signing in with a browser session is not affected. `POST /tokens/` is where a token with this scope is minted.

OrganizationFilter.description:
The narrowings a client may ask for on the organization list.

`name` is `icontains` for the same reason the example app's is: "find the
branch I half-remember" is the real question. `depth` is exact — it is a
small integer and a range would invite a client to ask for the whole tree
one level at a time.
OrganizationFilter.title: OrganizationFilter

OrganizationOut.description:
One node of a tenant's org tree, as both doors return it.

`path` and `depth` are on the wire because they are what makes the tree
legible to a client without a second round trip: `depth` says how far down
this node sits, and `path` sorts a flat list back into tree order. They are
read-only everywhere — the services own those columns (house rule 24), and
there is no `In` schema that carries either.
OrganizationOut.title: OrganizationOut

OrganizationIn.description:
A new node, under a parent the caller names.

`parent_id` is required and there is no default, deliberately: "create it
under the root" is a decision, and a create that silently chose the root
when a client forgot would put a branch in a place nobody asked for.
OrganizationIn.title: OrganizationIn

OrganizationPatch.description:
A rename, and only a rename.

The slug is absent on purpose: it is the handle `X-Org` names, so changing
it silently invalidates every stored header, every bookmark and every
script. `move` is absent for the opposite reason — it is a verb with a
workflow behind it, and it has its own route.
OrganizationPatch.title: OrganizationPatch

OrganizationMoveIn.description: Where a subtree is going. One field, because that is the whole decision.
OrganizationMoveIn.title: OrganizationMoveIn

MembershipFilter.description: Narrow by role, or by the branch a membership is held on.
MembershipFilter.title: MembershipFilter

MembershipOut.description:
Who belongs where, and as what.

`user_email` rather than a nested user shape: a membership answers "which
person, which branch, which role", and the person's own record is the
accounts door's business. It is resolved off the related row, which is why
every list here `select_related`s the user — and why the query pin in the
tests is what turns a lost `select_related` into a failure rather than a
slow page.
MembershipOut.title: MembershipOut

MembershipIn.description:
A person, a branch, a role.

The role a caller names is bounded at the write by the granter's own
ceiling (house rule 29) — this schema carries what was *asked for*, and
`add_membership` decides whether the asker could have granted it.
MembershipIn.title: MembershipIn

MembershipRolePatch.description: The one column a membership update may move.
MembershipRolePatch.title: MembershipRolePatch

RoleFilter.description: Narrow the role list by which layer owns it, or by a word in it.
RoleFilter.title: RoleFilter

RoleOut.description:
One role, from whichever of the three layers owns it.

`kind` is which layer: `owner` is the platform's one role and IS the
vocabulary, `declared` is a role an app named in its `roles.py`, `custom` is
a row this tenant made for itself. The distinction is on the wire because it
decides what a caller may do with the row — a declared role's collection can
be adjusted and its name cannot, and a custom role is the other way round.

`permissions` is the EFFECTIVE collection in this tenant;
`default_permissions` is the declaration's own half (`null` for a custom
role, which has no code layer to differ from), and `added`/`removed` are the
difference. A reader gets "what this role does here" and "what this tenant
changed" without computing either.
RoleOut.title: RoleOut

RoleIn.description:
A role this tenant is making for itself.

`permissions` accepts fnmatch PATTERNS as well as keys — `"*.read"` is how a
role is given every read this deployment has — and they are expanded to keys
at write time, so the row that lands names real permissions and a pattern
that matches nothing is refused rather than stored.
RoleIn.title: RoleIn

RolePatch.description:
The two columns a role's own row may move. **Never the key** (§D10).

A membership, a pending invitation and every delta row join on the key, so
renaming it would be a migration of three tables; the display name is the
renamable half by construction.
RolePatch.title: RolePatch

RolePermissionsIn.description:
What a role holds, as the WHOLE set rather than a diff.

A caller sends the collection they want and the server works out the delta —
which is what makes the request idempotent and what lets a declared role
keep its code layer underneath. Patterns are expanded exactly as on create.
RolePermissionsIn.title: RolePermissionsIn

GrantOut.description:
One exception standing on one membership.

`organization_id` is the membership's node, which is what makes this row an
answer to "where" as well as "what" — an exception granted in one branch
says nothing about the branch beside it.

`sentence` travels beside the key because the key is a word for this
codebase and the sentence is the one a person reads.

sentence.example: You may not approve that widget.
sentence.title: Sentence

GrantOut.title: GrantOut

example.sentence: You may not approve that widget.

items.sentence: You may not approve that widget.

GrantIn.description:
Which way the exception points. `allow` widens, `withhold` narrows.

One field, because the membership and the permission are in the path: a
grant is addressed rather than described, which is what makes `PUT` the
honest verb for it.
GrantIn.title: GrantIn

HeldPermissionOut.description:
One key somebody holds, and where it came from.

`via` is `role`, `grant` or `inherited`; on `inherited`, `membership_id`
names the ANCESTOR membership that carries it rather than the one asked
about, because "a role you hold further up the tree" is the answer and a
screen that pointed at this row would be pointing at the wrong one.

sentence.example: You may not approve that widget.
sentence.title: Sentence

HeldPermissionOut.title: HeldPermissionOut

example.sentence: You may not approve that widget.

MembershipPermissionsOut.description:
**The one read every permissions screen needs.**

What this membership may do at its own node, each key with its provenance,
and separately what has been taken away. A withhold is kept rather than
subtracted-and-forgotten: it is a decision somebody made, and the screen
that hides it is the screen where "why has this stopped working" has no
answer.
MembershipPermissionsOut.title: MembershipPermissionsOut

PermissionFilter.description: Narrow the vocabulary by kind, verb, who decided it, or a word in it.
PermissionFilter.title: PermissionFilter

items.sentence: You may not approve that widget.

PermissionOut.description:
One key in the vocabulary, with everything a role editor needs to choose it.

`decided_by` is the honest half: `derived` means the model registry produced
this key and nobody typed it, `declared` means an app's prose did, `reserved`
means the platform did and only `owner` holds it.

`has_row_predicate` says whether holding the key is the whole answer: a key
with a predicate is also asked about the ROW, so a role that names it grants
the capability and not the outcome.

sentence.example: You may not approve that widget.

InvitationFilter.description: Narrow the invitation list by status, the address invited, or the branch.
InvitationFilter.title: InvitationFilter

InvitationOut.description:
An outstanding invitation. **The token is not on this shape.**

A pending invitation's plaintext token is a bearer credential: whoever holds
it becomes a member. It is returned exactly once, by the issue route, in
`InvitationIssuedOut`, and never again by a list or a read — a list route
that carried it would turn "who have we invited" into "hand me every
outstanding credential".
InvitationOut.title: InvitationOut

InvitationIssuedOut.description:
The one answer that carries the token, at the one moment it exists.

`invite_member` returns the row and the plaintext together and stores only a
hash, so this is the only shape in the product that can ever show it. A
caller that loses it issues a new invitation; there is no route that will
tell them again, and that is the point.
InvitationIssuedOut.title: InvitationIssuedOut

InvitationIn.description:
Who to invite, where, and as what.

`organization_id` omitted is the ACTING HAT and never the tenant's root
(ADR core-20): an offer made from a branch is an offer of a place in that
branch. The door resolves a named id through the hat's own subtree, so a
node outside it is `not_found` rather than a placement — a caller can only
ever be surprised narrower.
InvitationIn.title: InvitationIn

InvitationAcceptIn.description:
The token from the link, and nothing else.

No tenant, no email, no user id: the token names the invitation and the
session names the person. A shape that let a caller say who they were
accepting *as* is the impersonation ADR core-16 keeps off the machine door.
InvitationAcceptIn.title: InvitationAcceptIn

TenantSettingsOut.description:
A tenant's own configuration, as both doors return it.

`settings` is the free-form half and `timezone`/`locale` are the two the
template itself reads — they are columns rather than settings keys because
the product renders dates with them, and a typo in a JSON key would be a
silently wrong timestamp instead of a refusal.

**`flags` is deliberately not here.** Feature flags have their own route and
their own shape, because they resolve against deployment defaults and a
settings read that folded them in would answer a different question than
the flags route does.
TenantSettingsOut.title: TenantSettingsOut

TenantSettingsIn.description:
What a caller may change about their own tenant.

`values` is **merged at the top level**, not replaced — a key set to `null`
is removed, which is how a client clears one. That is `update_tenant_settings`'s
grammar and this schema does not invent a second one.

`name`, `slug` and `status` are absent: a rename is a bigger decision than a
settings PUT, and status is what `suspend_tenant`/`close_tenant` move.
TenantSettingsIn.title: TenantSettingsIn

FlagsOut.description:
Every flag this tenant resolves, and what it resolves to.

The map is the union of the deployment's declared defaults and the tenant's
own overrides, so a client sees every flag that exists rather than only the
ones somebody has touched. `enabled_for` is the one resolver; this shape is
its answer.
FlagsOut.title: FlagsOut

FlagIn.description:
Set one flag, or clear the tenant's opinion of it.

`enabled: null` is **not** `false`. It removes the tenant's override so the
flag falls back to the deployment default — "we have no opinion" and "we
say no" are different answers, and a client that could only send a boolean
could never say the first one.
FlagIn.title: FlagIn

UserOut.description:
A person, as the deactivation and erasure doors hand them back.

**What is not here is the point.** `is_superuser` is the deployment's own
business and no tenant's; the identity platform's subjects (the identity
join, `SsoIdentity`) are not here either, because naming one over the wire
would hand a caller the key to somebody's account on it; `password` is a
hash and there is no door in this repository that returns one.

`email` **is** here, and it is what makes an erasure legible: the address
that comes back from `POST /users/{id}/erase` is the anonymised
`erased+<uuid>@erased.invalid` one, which is the caller's evidence that the act
landed rather than a copy of the person who used to be there.

RealmOut.description:
Where that address signs in — and nothing else about it.

**`method` is `sso` for every address** (ADR ident-6). Zitadel hosts
every interactive authentication now, including the passwords of local
users, so there is one door and the question "which door" has one answer.
`authorize_url` is always populated and always points at that door;
`connection_id` is present only when a live customer connection claims the
address's domain, in which case the URL also carries an opaque hint that
skips Zitadel's provider picker.

**The shape is unchanged and `password` stays in the vocabulary**, so a
client written against the previous contract still compiles and a product
that reopens a local password door has the word waiting for it.

**Everything a caller can learn from this is nothing.** No tenant name, no
slug, no connection name, no indication of whether an account exists, and no
difference between "that domain has no SSO", "that customer's connection is
disabled" and "we have never seen that domain" — all three are byte-
identical. A login form has to answer *something*, and the answer must not
be enumerable into a customer list.
RealmOut.title: RealmOut

MessageIn.description:
What a client may ask us to send.

`template` is a **name**, not an id: the caller asks for "the invoice
reminder", and `send()` resolves the latest active version for the tenant.
A caller that could name a version could pin a retired one for ever.

`context` is free-form by nature — it is the template's variables — and it
is validated against that template's `context_schema` inside `send()`,
before anything is written.

**Either a template or a policy, never both** (C2-comms-b). `policy` names
an escalation — *text them, wait, then email* — and its first step already
says which template on which channel, so naming one alongside it is a
caller who means two different things at once and is refused by name rather
than silently resolved one way. The three are optional *on the schema* and
the pairing is decided in `send()`, in one place, so the machine door and a
management command get the same refusal as the HTTP door.

`channel` therefore no longer defaults to `"email"` here — it defaults in
`send()`, which is where it always meant something. A body that omits it
still sends email, exactly as before.
MessageIn.title: MessageIn

MessageEngagementOut.description:
One thing a provider says a person did with a message.

The read shape of a `MessageEngagement` row, and the payload of
`comms.message.opened` and `comms.message.clicked` — the same shape at both,
for the reason `MessageOut` is: a webhook subscriber and a REST client
reading the same fact should not be reading two shapes that drift.

No field aliases, for `MessageOut`'s reason (see the note there): the MCP
transport serialises by alias, so an aliased field answers with a different
key at the machine door than at the human one.

`organization_id` is on it because house rule 38 requires it of every `Out`
of an `OrgScopedModel` — the socket fan-out narrows on that key and nothing
else, so a shape that omitted it would emit an event no branch owns and the
bridge would deliver it to every socket in the tenant. Here it is also the
load-bearing one: the row's organization is the MESSAGE's branch and not the
root the webhook acted at, which is `derive_org_from` doing its job all the
way out to the wire.

**`status` is deliberately not on this shape**, and its absence is the
contract: an engagement says nothing about whether the message arrived, so a
client that wants delivery truth reads `MessageOut`. Two shapes, because
they are two facts (ADR comms-9).
MessageEngagementOut.title: MessageEngagementOut
