PolicyStepIn.description:
One rung a caller asks for. **The service still decides it is legal.**

Pydantic checks the *shape* — the four fields, the types, a non-negative
wait — and `services._policy_steps` checks the *meaning*: that the channel
is a kind this product knows, that the template exists and is on that
channel, and that `escalate_when` is one of the closed two. Both, and not
one: the schema refusal is what makes a typo a 400 with the field named, and
the service refusal is what makes a policy written by a management command
or a test just as safe as one written through the door.

ArchivedByOut.description:
WHO pressed *Archive* — an id and a name, never an address.

The id is there while the person is; `name` is the user's `full_name` when
the product's user model carries one, and `null` otherwise — which tells a
screen to resolve the id, exactly as it does on the roster. No address is
published: the roster is the one read that carries one.
ArchivedByOut.title: ArchivedByOut

RecipientOut.description:
One contact, as every door reports it — and as `comms.recipient.archived`
and `comms.recipient.restored` carry it, less its `allowed_acts`.

`archived_at` and `archived_by` are inherited from `ArchivedOut`, never
re-declared: null unless the contact has been closed, and on the read shape
because "why is this person not in my list any more, and who closed them"
is the question they answer.

`allowed_acts` is inherited from `ActsOut`: the verbs THIS viewer may press
on this contact as it stands, set by `core.verbs.with_allowed_acts` on the
two viewer doors (a list page through `ActsPagination`, every other answer
for its one row). It describes the viewer, not the contact, so an event
payload never carries it — a subscriber is somebody else.
RecipientOut.title: RecipientOut

RecipientIn.description:
A new contact. The **organization is not on this shape** and never is.

Where a contact lands is decided by the acting hat the door resolved, not by
the caller: an `organization` field here would let a client write a row into
a branch it holds no membership over.
RecipientIn.title: RecipientIn

RecipientPatch.description:
A partial correction: absent means "leave it alone", not "set it to null".

Four fields, and the absences are still the design. `archived_at` is not
here — closing a contact is `POST .../archive/` and reopening it
`POST .../restore/`, verbs, so the audit row says what happened rather than
which column moved — and neither is anything
on the person's preferences, which is the consent surface and is only
reachable through its own five verbs.

`phone` and `chat_handle` are here because they are **addresses, not
consent**: knowing somebody's number is not permission to text them, and an
escalation that reaches for SMS still meets the whole wall at that step's
own send time.
RecipientPatch.title: RecipientPatch

PreferenceOut.description:
What one person has agreed to on one channel, as every door reports it.

`has_marketing_consent` is a property on the model rather than a field here,
so the "yes and not since revoked" comparison is made in one place and both
timestamps stay on the shape beside it — a client that has to prove consent
to a regulator needs the dates, and one that has to decide whether to show a
checkbox needs the answer.
PreferenceOut.title: PreferenceOut

PreferenceIn.description:
Which channel a consent verb is about. The verb is the route, not a field.

There is no `suppressed_at`, no `marketing_consented_at` and no
`marketing_revoked_at` here — a column a door can set is a column a door can
set *back*, and a consent timestamp somebody typed is not a consent record.
PreferenceIn.title: PreferenceIn

QuietHoursIn.description:
The window, in the person's own timezone. Both ends, or neither.

Neither is how quiet hours are turned off; one is a window nobody can
evaluate, and the service refuses it with the field named.
QuietHoursIn.title: QuietHoursIn

DeviceOut.description:
One registered device, as every door reports it.

**No token material, of any kind, in any field** — not the token, not a
prefix, not a digest. That is the contract and not an omission: a push
registration token is the capability to put a notification on somebody's
lock screen, `Device.push_token` is encrypted at rest for that reason, and a
read shape that handed a fragment back would undo the encryption for every
caller who can list. This schema is also the payload of
`comms.device.registered` and `comms.device.retired`, so it travels to
every webhook endpoint a tenant has configured — which is the wire that
makes the rule non-negotiable rather than tidy.

A client that has just registered gets `id` back and addresses the device by
it from then on. `push_token_hash` is the database's identity for the row
and is deliberately not published either: it is a digest of a live
credential, and publishing one lets a holder of the token confirm which
tenant's contact it belongs to.

No field aliases, for `MessageOut`'s reason: the MCP transport serialises by
alias and an aliased field answers with a different key at the machine door.
DeviceOut.title: DeviceOut

DeviceIn.description:
A device to push to. **The organization is not on this shape** and never is.

`RecipientIn`'s rule, and here it is not even a choice the door could make:
a `Device` declares `derive_org_from = "recipient"`, so the row lands
wherever the contact lives and the landing gate in `OrgScopedModel.clean()`
refuses anything else.

`push_token` is the platform's registration token, exactly as the client
received it — an FCM registration id, an APNs device token, a web-push
subscription. It is **not** validated into shape here for `Recipient.phone`'s
reason: the format is the gateway's and it changes when the gateway does, so
a validator here would refuse a real registration to enforce a guess. It is
stored encrypted and never comes back out on any door.

Re-sending an existing token is the **normal** case rather than an error —
a mobile client re-registers on every launch — so this is one route that
answers `200` with the row it found rather than `409`. See the route's own
contract.
DeviceIn.title: DeviceIn

WebhookEndpointFilter.description: The narrowings a client may ask for over its endpoints.
WebhookEndpointFilter.title: WebhookEndpointFilter

WebhookEndpointOut.description:
One endpoint, as every door reports it — **with no secret on it**.

The absence is the contract. Every read of an endpoint answers this shape,
so there is no route, tool, page or export anywhere that can hand a signing
key back: it is not that the key is filtered out, it is that no reader has a
field for it. `WebhookEndpointSecretOut` is the only shape that carries one.
WebhookEndpointOut.title: WebhookEndpointOut

WebhookEndpointSecretOut.description:
An endpoint **and the signing key, said once**.

Answered by exactly two acts — registering an endpoint and issuing it a new
key — and by nothing else, ever. The subscriber computes
`X-Signature: sha256=<hmac>` over the raw body it receives with this value;
we keep it encrypted at rest because a signature cannot be computed from a
hash, and we never read it back out through a door because a key that can be
read twice has leaked twice.
WebhookEndpointSecretOut.title: WebhookEndpointSecretOut

WebhookEndpointIn.description:
Where a tenant wants its events delivered.

There is **no secret field**, deliberately: the signing key is minted by the
server so that the only copy a client ever holds is the one the create
response hands back. A key a client chose is a key a client can have chosen
badly, and a key a client can send twice is a key that can be re-sent by
whoever read the first request.

`event_names` empty means every event — the honest default for "tell me what
happens here". A name that no installed app declares is refused against the
catalogue (`GET /catalogue/`), because a subscription to an event that does
not exist is a subscription that silently never fires.
WebhookEndpointIn.title: WebhookEndpointIn

WebhookEndpointPatch.description:
Change an endpoint's address, subscription or label. Omitted fields stay.

`is_active` is not here and never will be: pausing and resuming are verbs
on their own sub-paths, because a column a door can set is a column a door
can set back by accident. The signing key is not here either — it is issued,
never assigned.
WebhookEndpointPatch.title: WebhookEndpointPatch

EventTypeOut.description:
One event name this deployment can emit, and the app that declares it.

**Derived, never listed.** The population is read off the installed apps'
own `events.py` modules at request time (`events.declared_names()`), which
is the same registry `emit` validates against and the same one `introspect`
prints — so a subscriber picks from what actually exists, and the catalogue
cannot rot the day another app declares an event.
EventTypeOut.title: EventTypeOut

DeliveryFilter.description: The narrowings a client may ask for over its deliveries.
DeliveryFilter.title: DeliveryFilter

DeliveryOut.description:
One endpoint's attempt at one event — including the one that never landed.

`attempts` is the lineage: it counts every HTTP attempt this pair has had,
across the first dispatch and every replay, on the one row that is unique on
(endpoint, event). So a dead letter that has been replayed reads as a higher
`attempts` than the one that dead-lettered it, against the same
`dead_lettered_at` — which is what makes "was this ever sent again, and did
it land" a query rather than a log search.

`event_name` is a **property on `Delivery`** rather than a `resolve_` hook on
this schema, and the distinction is load-bearing. A ninja resolver is
consulted *before* plain attribute access on whatever object is being
validated — including a `DeliveryOut` instance being re-validated as an item
of `DeliveryPage`, which has no `event` to read through. So a resolver here
would work at the HTTP door and fail at the machine one, which is the
door-parity break this whole app is against. A property is found by both.
Comms' `MessageOut` avoids aliases for the same family of reason.
DeliveryOut.title: DeliveryOut

MeasuredBasisOut.description:
How a measured number was arrived at: the formula, and what went into it.

`formula` is a short human-readable string (`"gross - discounts - refunds"`,
`"closed / opened"`), and `inputs` are the named values it was evaluated
over. Between them a person can check the arithmetic without a second
request and without a second implementation.

**The example below is hand-written, and the arithmetic in it is real.**
A synthesised one is shaped right and says nothing — `formula` came
out as `"formula"` and `inputs` as `{}`, which is a published example of a
basis that explains nothing about a value it does not contain. The one here
is the same sum `MeasuredOut`'s example resolves, so a reader who checks the
subtraction gets the answer the sibling field shows.
MeasuredBasisOut.title: MeasuredBasisOut

MeasuredOut.description:
A number the server computed, **with its basis attached** (ADR core-7).

    MeasuredOut(
        value=Decimal("1240.50"),
        basis=MeasuredBasisOut(
            formula="gross - discounts",
            inputs={"gross": Decimal("1400.00"), "discounts": Decimal("159.50")},
        ),
    )

The contract is one sentence: **a number the UI never computes.** The
alternative — ship the parts and let each door add them up — is how a
dashboard, an export and an assistant come to disagree about revenue while
every one of them is reading the same rows. It was honoured 104 times by
convention in the product this was lifted from, which is a convention
worth making a type.

`Decimal`, not `float`, at both levels: house rule 15, and money that
round-trips through a float is money that stops adding up. Pydantic renders
a `Decimal` as a **string** in `model_dump(mode="json")` and on the wire, so
the value that arrives is the value that was computed.

The `Out` suffix is rule 16's grammar; ADR core-7's prose says `Measured`/`MeasuredBasis`.

**Enforcement is at criteria-tier, honestly** (ADR core-7): "any endpoint
returning a computed aggregate" is an open set, and no closed question can
scope it. The engineering lead's checklist carries the line; there is no
AST rule pretending to recognise an aggregate, and that blind spot is
declared rather than disguised.

**Its own example is hand-written and its arithmetic is real.** The
synthesised one published `{"value": "value", …}`, which does not validate
against this very schema — a published example a client cannot paste back is
an instrument that is wrong about the one thing it exists to show. The value
below is exactly what `MeasuredBasisOut`'s example evaluates to, and
`apps/core/tests/test_published_examples.py` recomputes the subtraction
rather than trusting the two strings to have been typed consistently.
MeasuredOut.title: MeasuredOut

ExportFilter.description:
The narrowings a client may ask for, declared rather than improvised.

A `FilterSchema` is how ninja turns query parameters into a `Q` without any
route reading `request.GET` — which is where filtering usually goes wrong,
because a hand-rolled filter reaches into `.filter(**request.GET)` and lets
a client query any column and traverse any relation.

`status` is an exact match: it is a word from a closed vocabulary, and a
substring match on it would make `?status=fail` quietly mean `failed`.
ExportFilter.title: ExportFilter

ExportOut.description:
What a client gets back for one export.

**The two download fields are a pair and a client reads them as one.**
`download_url` is a short-lived presigned link straight to object storage;
`download_path` is this API's own authenticated route, which answers `302`
with that same link. Both are present whenever there is an archive and both
are `null` until then, so `download_url or download_path` is right as it
always was — which is why there is still no third field saying which kind of
deployment this is. (Before XPr the pair really did vary: `download_url` was
absent where `default_storage` could not sign. The archive now lives in the
files seam, which refuses a deployment that has named no bucket, so the
signing branch is the only one left and the pair has become a redundancy a
client already handles rather than a fork it has to.)

`manifest` is deliberately on the read shape rather than behind a second
request: it is how a client knows what the archive contains — which tables,
how many rows each, which columns were left out and why, and which tables a
subtree export could not carry. A client that had to download a multi-
gigabyte zip to find out it was missing a table would find out too late.
ExportOut.title: ExportOut

ExportIn.description:
What a client may send to ask for an archive.

There is no `organization` on this list and its absence is the enforcement:
an export lands at the organization the request was made under — the `X-Org`
header, or your default one — so no body can put one somewhere the caller is
not a member.

There is no `models` list either, and that is deliberate rather than
unfinished. An export is "everything you can see", derived from the model
registry (`apps/exports/census.py`), and a client that could name the tables
would be a client whose archive silently stops covering the table somebody
added on Thursday — which is the exact failure the derived census exists to
prevent, moved from the server to the caller.

scope.description: How much to export: `organization` for everything the organization you are acting as can see, `tenant` for the whole account.
scope.title: Scope

idempotency_key.description: Your own name for this request. Sending the same one twice returns the first export instead of building a second archive.
idempotency_key.title: Idempotency Key

ExportIn.title: ExportIn

FileFilter.description:
The narrowings a client may ask for, declared rather than improvised.

A `FilterSchema` is how ninja turns query parameters into a `Q` without any
route reading `request.GET` — which is where filtering usually goes wrong,
because a hand-rolled filter reaches into `.filter(**request.GET)` and lets a
client query any column and traverse any relation.

`purpose` is an exact match: it is a label a product chose, and a substring
match would make `?purpose=export` quietly mean `export-archive` too.
`filename` is a containment match, because a filename is what a person
remembers half of.
FileFilter.title: FileFilter

StoredFileOut.description:
One document, as `files.file.stored` and every read door report it.

`current_version` is `0` until the first version finalizes. That is a real
state, not a placeholder: a document whose only version is still pending has
no current bytes, and a subscriber that sees `0` should read it as "nothing is
downloadable yet" rather than as version one.

**`archived_at` and `archived_by` are inherited from `ArchivedOut`, never
re-declared** — every archivable noun publishes the one archive shape, and
house rule 74 reads the inheritance.

**`allowed_acts` is inherited from `ActsOut`** — the verbs the acting hat may
press on THIS document as it stands (an archived one offers `restore`; a member
is offered no `archive`), set by `core.verbs.with_allowed_acts` on both viewer
doors and never computed by a client. It answers one viewer, so it never rides
an event: every payload this app emits is dumped without it.

filename.description: The display name. Renaming it moves no bytes.

FileVersionOut.description:

`size_bytes` and `sha256` are **what this platform measured** by streaming the
object, never what an uploader declared — see `models.FileVersion`. They are
`None` and empty respectively until the version is `stored`, which is the
honest answer while an upload is still outstanding rather than a zero that
reads like a measurement.

organization_id.description: The part of the organization the document this version belongs to lives in.
organization_id.title: Organization Id

version.description: The ordinal, counting from 1. Version 1 is never re-issued.
version.title: Version

content_type.description: What the uploader said the bytes are. Advisory, and never evidence.
content_type.title: Content Type

size_bytes.description: What we measured, in bytes. Null until the bytes have landed.
size_bytes.title: Size Bytes

sha256.description: The hex SHA-256 we computed by streaming the object. Empty until stored.

uploaded_by_id.description: Who uploaded this version — not the same question as who filed the document.
uploaded_by_id.title: Uploaded By Id

UploadTicketOut.description:
A place to put one version's bytes, and the two headers the PUT must carry.

What `POST /files/` and `POST /files/{id}/versions` answer with. **The URL is
in this answer and nowhere else** — it is a signature with an expiry, and a
signature written to a column is a credential at rest — so re-reading the
document later will not give it back to you. Ask again and a fresh one is
minted and audited.

**The PUT is signed for exactly two headers and both are required.** Send
`Content-Type` set to the value you declared here, and `If-None-Match: *`,
which is the store's own way of saying *write only if nothing is there*. SigV4
covers the header set, so omitting either is not a lenient upload — it is a
signature over a request you did not make, and the store refuses it before a
byte lands. That belt is also what stops a leaked upload URL from replacing
bytes that have already been finalized and digested.

Then call `POST /files/{id}/versions/{n}/confirm`. Nothing is stored until the
platform has been round and measured the object itself.

upload_url.description: Where to PUT the bytes. Short-lived, and issued once.
upload_url.title: Upload Url

expires_in.description: How many seconds the upload URL is good for.
expires_in.title: Expires In

UploadTicketOut.title: UploadTicketOut

What a client sends to file a new document.

There is no `organization` on this list and its absence is the enforcement: a
document lands at the organization the request was made under — the `X-Org`
header, or your default one — so no body can put one somewhere the caller is
not a member.

filename.description: What to call it. A label for people; nothing about the bytes depends on it.
filename.title: Filename

content_type.description: What you are about to upload. The presigned PUT is signed for this value.
content_type.title: Content Type

size_bytes.description: How big you expect it to be. Checked against the limit; never recorded.
size_bytes.title: Size Bytes

purpose.description: Your own short label for why it exists — `contract`, `lab-result`, anything.
purpose.title: Purpose

subject.description: The record to file this document against, as `<kind>:<id>`. It lands in that record's organization. Leave it out to file against nothing.
subject.title: Subject

FileDownloadOut.description:
Where one version's bytes are, for the few minutes after you asked.

What `POST /files/{id}/download-url` answers with, at both doors. It names the
version it signed for, which is the same version the audit row records: an
issuance is a witnessed act, and what was witnessed is *which bytes*, not
*which document*.

**The link is a bearer credential with no name on it.** Anyone holding it can
fetch those bytes until it expires, and nothing of ours sits in that request
path — so do not paste it anywhere durable, and do not store it. When it
expires the store answers `403` in its own words, un-re-dressed by us, and the
remedy is to ask here again rather than to look for a longer-lived link. There
is no longer-lived link, and re-issuing re-audits.

**A URL issued for version 2 keeps serving version 2's bytes** after version 3
lands and becomes current. Every version has its own object; promotion moves
which one a reader who names none gets, and never what an already-issued link
means.

version.description: The version these bytes are. Pinned at issuance and never re-pointed.
version.title: Version

download_url.description: A temporary link straight to storage. Needs no credential of yours.
download_url.title: Download Url

expires_in.description: How many seconds the link is good for.
expires_in.title: Expires In

content_type.description: What the uploader declared the bytes are. Advisory.
content_type.title: Content Type

size_bytes.description: What we measured when we streamed the object.
size_bytes.title: Size Bytes

sha256.description: The digest we measured. Check the bytes you fetched against it.
sha256.title: Sha256

FileDownloadOut.title: FileDownloadOut

DownloadUrlIn.description:
What a client may send when asking for a link to the bytes.

Send nothing and you get the current version. Name a `version` and the link is
pinned to that one — useful when you recorded a digest and want the bytes it
was taken from, whatever has landed since.

version.description: Which version to sign for. Leave it out for the current one.
version.title: Version

DownloadUrlIn.title: DownloadUrlIn

There is no `filename` here: replacing a document does not rename it, and a
body that could would make "replace" two acts with one name.

content_type.title: Content Type

ConfirmUploadIn.description:
What a client sends to say the bytes are up.

`idempotency_key` is **your own name for the unit of work**, and it is
required: a confirm with no key is a caller who has not thought about their own
retries. It is not what stops a double confirm — the verification run's id is
derived from the version, so a second confirm joins the first run rather than
starting one — it is what ties this call to whatever you were doing in your own
system, on the audit row and in the log line.

idempotency_key.description: Your own name for this upload. Rides onto the audit row.
idempotency_key.title: Idempotency Key

One kind of thing this product can search, and the part of it that owns them.

Derived from the registry at request time, so it is complete and current for
the build answering — never a hand-kept list. The same for every customer:
it says what the PRODUCT can find, not what you happen to have.

SearchPage.description:
One page of results, in the envelope every list here uses (ADR core-18).

`items`, `has_more`, `next_cursor` and `count` are the standard envelope:
walk with `?cursor=`, stop when `has_more` is false, and `count` is `null`
unless you sent `?include_count=true`. The cursor is opaque — it names a
position in *this* ranked result set, so it is not interchangeable with a
list endpoint's cursor and the API says so rather than misreading one.

`engine` is search's own field and it is on the wire on purpose. Search
degrades rather than failing: when the index is unreachable the product
answers from Postgres instead — slower, plainer, and still correctly scoped
— and a caller that wants to say "results may be incomplete" can. A caller
that does not care ignores it. What neither has to do is guess.

engine.description: Which engine answered: `meili` normally, `postgres` while the index is unreachable. The results are scoped identically either way. A page that was answered without asking any engine — because you can see nothing here — still names the engine this deployment searches with, so that a page you are not entitled to and a page that matched nothing cannot be told apart.
engine.title: Engine

SearchPage.title: SearchPage

PeriodKind.description:
The windows a total is asked for over. Two, and adding a third is a diff.

A `StrEnum` because these values are written by hand into a tenant's settings
JSON and read back out of it: `"month"` in the config file and
`PeriodKind.MONTH` in the code have to be the same object without anybody
mapping between them.

**No `year`, no `week`, no arbitrary range** — not because they are hard, but
because every one of them is a bucketing decision a rollup will one day have
to materialise, and the set that gets materialised should be the set somebody
chose. A caller wanting an arbitrary window builds a `Period` directly.
PeriodKind.title: PeriodKind

UsageReportOut.description:
What one window of the ledger says, per meter, **with the arithmetic shown**.

The whole of the read door's answer (ADR usage-1, § Doors). `meters` maps a
meter name to its `MeasuredOut`, so a caller gets the total *and* the day
subtotals it was summed from and never has to add anything up to agree with
the server — the failure ADR core-7 exists to prevent is a dashboard, an
export and an assistant each computing a customer's consumption differently
from the same rows.

**The window is on the wire and not implied.** A report that answered only
numbers would leave a reader to work out which month "this month" was in the
server's timezone; `period`, `starts_on` and `ends_on` say it. The window is
UTC and half-open internally, so `ends_on` is the last day the report covers
rather than the first day it does not — an inclusive date is what a person
reading "1 August to 31 August" expects, and a report that said
`2026-09-01` would be read as covering a day it does not.

**Every quantity here is a quantity, never a price.** A meter counts things
consumed — tokens, bytes, messages — and what any of them costs is a
product-layer decision this app deliberately does not hold.
UsageReportOut.title: UsageReportOut

MeterOut.description:
One meter this deployment declares, and the app that declares it.

**Derived, never listed** — the same shape and the same argument as
`events.schemas.EventTypeOut`, because it is the same kind of thing: a
published vocabulary read off the installed apps' own `meters.py` modules at
request time (`usage.meters.declared_meters()`). That is the registry
`record_usage` validates a write against and the registry the read door now
refuses an unknown name against, so a caller picks from what actually
exists and the catalogue cannot rot the day another app declares a meter.

Two fields and no third. There is no `description` here and it is not an
omission: a meter's declaration is a string constant, its meaning is the
declaring module's docstring, and a description field would be a second
place to say what `files.storage.bytes` counts — one that a reviewer of
`apps/files/meters.py` would never see go stale.
MeterOut.title: MeterOut

MeterPage.description:
A page of the vocabulary, in the list envelope both doors use (ADR core-18).

**Both doors return this class**, rather than REST returning `list[MeterOut]`
through `@paginate` and MCP returning a hand-built twin. Two reasons, and the
second is the one that decided it:

* parity stops being a thing to prove and becomes a thing that is true — one
  schema, one `cursor_page` call, no `Paged...` wrapper ninja builds for one
  door and not the other (`apps/search/api.py` takes the same shape, for its
  own reason: no queryset for a paginator to slice, and there is none here
  either — the population is a registry walk);
* `items` can carry a **declared example**. A `@paginate`d route's wrapper is
  built as `type(f"Paged{X}", (paginator.Output,), ...)`, which re-annotates
  `items` and drops any example declared on `ListPage.items` — so every
  paginated route in this tree contributes one undeclarable field to house
  rule 41's census, and `quality/rules.yaml` says so at length under
  `undeclared_example_fields` (it names the real fix, in `core.api.docs`, as
  somebody else's line). A vocabulary door that raised that ratchet to
  publish a two-field catalogue would be paying a real cost for nothing.
MeterPage.title: MeterPage

tags.name: auth
tags.description: Where an email address signs in, asked before anybody is signed in — and the tenant's own identity-provider configuration, which decides who may join it and at what role. That makes it the most powerful thing in this API, and it is owner-or-administrator only. No client secret is ever in a response.

tags.name: connections
tags.description: This tenant's links to outside systems: registering a provider, the OAuth round trip, storing and revoking credentials, and the signed inbound webhook the provider calls back on. Credentials are stored encrypted and no response here ever carries one out.

tags.name: devices
tags.description: The push address book: the handsets and browsers a contact has let this product notify. Registering a device says the product CAN reach it and never that it MAY — consent, quiet hours and suppression for the `push` channel live with the other consent verbs under Messaging & contacts, and every notification is checked against them. Registration tokens are stored encrypted and are never published on any door or in any event.

tags.name: djb_imports
tags.description: Bringing rows in from a CSV file. Stage a file you have uploaded, read the preview of what it would do — every row checked, nothing written — and apply it. Rows the preview refused are listed with the reason and skipped; the rest apply. Staging the same file twice gives you the same import.

tags.name: djb_notes
tags.description: Notes about any record that takes them. A note names the record it is about as `<kind>:<id>` and lives where that record lives, so it is visible to exactly the people who can see the record. Notes are listed through the record they are about, edited only by the person who wrote them, and archived rather than deleted.

tags.name: djb_tags
tags.description: The tenant's shared words, and the rows that carry them. Coin a tag once for the whole tenant, put it on any row that takes tags by naming the row as `<kind>:<id>`, read a row's tags the same way, and take a tag off again. Retiring a word hides it from the list and keeps it on every row that already carries it.

tags.name: events
tags.description: Webhook subscriptions and what became of them: where a tenant's events are delivered, which events exist to subscribe to, and every delivery attempt including the ones that gave up. The signing key is answered once, when it is minted, and is never readable again — every other read of an endpoint has no field for it.

tags.name: exports
tags.description: Taking a copy of your data out of the product. Ask for an archive of everything your organization can see — or, with administrator rights, of the whole account — follow it while it is built, and download it. Archives are deleted automatically after a month.

tags.name: files
tags.description: Documents you store with us and the versions they have had. Put a document in, replace it later without losing what it used to say, and fetch any version back on a short-lived private link. The bytes never travel through this API — you upload and download straight to storage — and every link we issue is recorded against the version it was issued for.

tags.name: invitations
tags.description: Bringing somebody into the tenant: issuing an invitation at a branch and a role, revoking one, and the link that accepts it. An invitation records the branch it was issued from and the membership lands exactly there, so an invitation can never be a way to place somebody above the person who sent it. Accepting is a browser act — the link names the invitation and the session names the person — and it is the one capability here with no machine-door twin.

tags.name: messaging
tags.description: Sending, and everything that decides whether a send is allowed to happen: the message log, versioned templates and delivery policies, the contact book, and per-person consent, quiet hours and suppression. Consent, quiet hours and suppression are applied to every message this API sends, so a send to somebody who has opted out is refused rather than delivered.

tags.name: org-structure
tags.description: A tenant's organization tree: the branches, divisions or franchisees it is divided into, how they nest, and what each one is called. Reads are narrowed to the subtree your `X-Org` hat covers and writes are bounded by the role you hold over the branch they land in — so a branch manager reshapes their own branch and cannot see or rename anything outside it. Who belongs to which branch is a different section: see **Roles & members**.

tags.name: portal_requests
tags.description: What customers ask about the widgets they can see. A request names one widget and says, in the customer's words, what they want; it lives where the customer was acting when they sent it, so they read it back and the staff above them read it too. Requests are sent and read; nobody edits one.

tags.name: roles
tags.description: Who belongs to which part of the tenant, and as what. Granting, changing and removing a person's role — the access-control decisions themselves, kept apart from the tree they are made against so a credential trusted to reshape the structure is not thereby trusted to promote anybody. Nobody grants above their own ceiling, and a role is bounded at the branch it lands in.

tags.name: runs
tags.description: Background jobs. Work this API does not finish while you wait — sending a message, syncing an integration, onboarding a record — is started as a background job, and every one of them appears here: what it was, who started it, whether it is still running, and why it failed if it did. A job of your own that failed can be restarted from the beginning with the input it was originally given. There is no endpoint here for nudging a job that is waiting on something, or for changing how hard it retries: those belong to whichever endpoint started the job.

tags.name: search
tags.description: Finding things by typing words. One endpoint searches everything your organization can see, across every kind of record this product has made searchable, and answers with pointers you can then fetch in full.

tags.name: socket-tickets
tags.description: The event socket at `ws/events/`, and the one-use ticket a client presents to open it. A credential never travels in the socket's URL: a browser signed in by cookie opens the socket as it is, and every other client mints a ticket here first.

tags.name: tenant-settings
tags.description: The tenant's own configuration: its name, time zone and locale, the free-form `settings` object your application keeps its own configuration in, and the feature flags that turn product behaviour on and off. Configuration applies to everybody in the tenant, so changing any of it asks for `admin` or `owner` over the tenant as a whole rather than over one branch of it.

tags.name: tokens
tags.description: Bearer tokens, so a program can call this API as you. Minted from a signed-in browser session and pinned to the tenant you were acting in, shown **exactly once**, and revoked by a route that keeps the record so what the token did is still attributable. There is no route that reads a token back.

tags.name: usage
tags.description: What this account has consumed, measured and shown. Every meter is a count of things used — tokens, bytes, messages — reported for a day or a month with the daily subtotals it was added up from. Meters record quantities and never prices, and nothing here can be written: usage is recorded by the platform as it happens, and a figure you disagree with is a conversation with us rather than a request you can send.

tags.name: users
tags.description: Taking a person's access away. **Deactivation is reversible and erasure is not**: deactivating switches an account off and changes nothing else, while erasing replaces the person's email address with an unreachable one and cannot be undone by anybody. Each act has two routes — `/users/me/...` acts on you and can name nobody else, and `/users/{user_id}/...` acts on someone in the tenant you are signed in to. Both routes behave identically and allow the same callers: you, over your own account, or an administrator of your whole tenant. Nothing here deletes an account, so records that refer to the person keep reading correctly afterwards.

tags.name: widgets
tags.description: The worked example: one org-scoped resource end to end. Widgets show the house shapes a product copies — a filtered, searched, ordered, paginated list; a create that names a policy it must be able to reach; a verb on a sub-path rather than a settable column; an append-only ledger; and a measured count that travels with the arithmetic that produced it.
